For example, the Result from an authenticated `tools/list` call with a `"public"` `cacheScope` may be cached by a client and may be shared outside of the initial request's authorization context (i.e. different access tokens can leverage the same cache).

q.en: A tools/list result contains fewer entries for a user with a narrower OAuth scope than for an administrator calling the same server. Does this violate the requirement that list results must not vary per connection?

o.en: No, but only if the two users happen to be using two different transports entirely
No, since list results may vary by the authorization on the request, just not by the connection itself
Yes, unless the administrator explicitly and repeatedly calls tools/list twice over before the comparison ever finally becomes valid
Yes, since any variation at all in a list result is forbidden under the stateless core

x.en: The stateless core forbids list results from varying as a side effect of the connection or prior requests, but it explicitly allows variation by the authorization presented on a request. Two different scopes producing two different lists is exactly that permitted case, not a violation.

questions.setTitle: MCPA Full-Length Mock 3: Design and Security Trade-offs

cite.text: Servers that declare the `tools` capability MUST respond to `tools/list` requests with the set of tools currently available to the requesting client. This set MAY be empty and MAY change over time (see List Changed Notification), but MUST NOT vary per-connection or as a side effect of other requests on the connection. The set MAY vary by the authorization presented on the request — for example, returning only the tools the caller's granted scopes permit — since credentials are per-request input, not connection state.

q.en: Which two statements correctly describe how a subscriptions/listen stream must behave under 2026-07-28? Select two.

o.en: The server may freely send any notification type on the stream even if the client never asked to filter for it
Every message on the stream carries a subscriptionId in _meta equal to the JSON-RPC id of the original listen request
A client must always fully reopen a fresh subscriptions/listen call before every single tool invocation it ever makes at all
The first message on the stream must be notifications/subscriptions/acknowledged, echoing the subset of notification types the server will actually honor

x.en: A listen stream opens with an acknowledgment naming what the server will honor, and every later message is tagged with the subscriptionId tying it back to that listen request's id. The server must never send unrequested notification types, and listening has no required relationship to individual tool calls.

questions.setTitle: MCPA Full-Length Mock 3: Design and Security Trade-offs

cite.text: The server acknowledges the subscription with `notifications/subscriptions/acknowledged`, which is the first message carrying that subscription's ID in `_meta` (the server sends no other notification for that subscription before it). Its `notifications` field reflects the subset of the requested filter the server agreed to honor, with unsupported notification types omitted:

q.en: A report-generation tool typically takes ten minutes to finish. A designer is choosing between a plain synchronous tools/call, an MRTR input_required exchange, and the tasks extension. Which fits, and why do the other two fail?

o.en: A plain synchronous call instead, since clients are generally expected to hold a connection open for as long as it ever takes
MRTR, since ten whole minutes of waiting is exactly what elicitation was originally built to fill with a prompt
The tasks extension, since a synchronous call risks timeouts and MRTR is for gathering input, not for waiting out work
None of the three, since long work must always be split into ten separate one-minute calls

x.en: A blocking synchronous call over ten minutes risks intermediary and client timeouts, and MRTR exists to gather input mid-flight, not to represent duration. The tasks extension is purpose built for durable long running work, returning a task handle the client polls instead of holding a connection open.

questions.setTitle: MCPA Full-Length Mock 3: Design and Security Trade-offs

cite.text: Not every tool call returns instantly. Some operations — CI pipelines, batch processing, human approvals — take seconds, minutes, or longer. MCP Tasks let servers return a durable handle instead of blocking, so clients can poll for progress, provide input when needed, and retrieve the final result after reconnecting.

q.en: A tool that runs a multi-step build pipeline needs to track progress across several minutes. Where should that intermediate state live: in requestState, inside the task object the tasks extension returns, or in ordinary server-side storage referenced by an opaque id?

o.en: In ordinary server-side storage only, and never expose any id to the client at all
In requestState alone, since it is specifically designed to carry any data a server wants to keep across calls indefinitely
Split evenly across all three separate locations so that a missing one still leaves a copy safely elsewhere
In the task object and server-side storage keyed by taskId, since requestState survives only one MRTR round trip

x.en: requestState exists to survive exactly one MRTR round trip and is explicitly never cached or reused beyond that, while the tasks extension's taskId and its backing server-side storage are the purpose built mechanism for state that spans a multi-step, minutes-long operation the client polls.

questions.setTitle: MCPA Full-Length Mock 3: Design and Security Trade-offs

cite.text: This example demonstrates how `requestState` enables a multi-round-trip elicitation flow driven by Azure DevOps custom rules. The scenario involves an `update_work_item` tool that transitions a Bug work item to "Resolved." ADO custom rules require specific fields when certain state transitions occur, and the server uses iterative elicitation to gather them — accumulating context in `requestState` across rounds so that the final update can be executed without any server-side storage.

q.en: A server author wants to add an application-defined error code meaning quota exceeded. Which numeric range is the correct place for it under the 2026-07-28 allocation policy?

o.en: Outside -32768 to -32000 entirely, since that whole band is reserved for JSON-RPC and MCP use
Anywhere in -32000 to -32019, since that legacy band is open for any implementation to reuse
Anywhere at all in -32020 to -32099, since that band is available for any server-specific extension error code
It does not matter, since JSON-RPC error codes are purely cosmetic and never machine interpreted

x.en: The allocation policy reserves -32000 to -32019 for legacy use only, -32020 to -32099 for the MCP specification itself, and directs application-defined codes outside the entire -32768 to -32000 band. A quota-exceeded code belongs outside that whole reserved range.

questions.setTitle: MCPA Full-Length Mock 3: Design and Security Trade-offs

cite.text: New error codes for purposes not defined by this specification SHOULD be allocated outside the JSON-RPC reserved range (`-32768` to `-32000`); the remainder of the integer space is available for application-defined errors.

q.en: A server currently uses the deprecated sampling capability to ask the client's model for a completion mid-tool-call. Which two statements correctly describe migrating away from it under 2026-07-28? Select two.

o.en: Sampling still functions as an MRTR input request today, so the migration can happen on the server's own schedule before removal
A client that has still not declared the sampling capability on a request can still be asked for a completion through it anyway
Sampling must be removed immediately, since deprecated features are stripped out of every server the moment a new revision ships
The recommended migration is for the server to call an LLM provider API directly instead of asking the client for a completion

x.en: Sampling is deprecated with a clear migration path, calling a provider API directly, but it remains functional through MRTR today, so teams can migrate on their own timeline rather than under immediate pressure. A client must still declare the capability before a server may request it.

questions.setTitle: MCPA Full-Length Mock 3: Design and Security Trade-offs

cite.text: Deprecated: The Sampling feature is deprecated as of protocol version `2026-07-28` (SEP-2577). Under the feature lifecycle policy, it remains in the specification for at least twelve months after this revision's release before it becomes eligible for removal. New implementations SHOULD NOT adopt it; existing implementations SHOULD migrate to integrating directly with LLM provider APIs. See the deprecated features registry.

q.en: Select the three failures that 2026-07-28 treats as JSON-RPC protocol errors rather than tool execution errors.

o.en: A tools/call whose arguments violate the target tool's own inputSchema
A tools/call naming a tool that the server does not expose at all
A request that is missing the required io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities per-request meta field
A request whose shape does not satisfy the CallToolRequest schema at all

x.en: An unknown tool, a request that fails the CallToolRequest schema, and a request missing required per-request metadata are all protocol level failures returned as JSON-RPC errors. Arguments that merely violate a specific tool's inputSchema are, by contrast, a tool execution error the model can read and correct.

questions.setTitle: MCPA Full-Length Mock 3: Design and Security Trade-offs

cite.text: Tools use two error reporting mechanisms: Protocol Errors (unknown tool, malformed requests, server errors) are returned as standard JSON-RPC errors; Tool Execution Errors (API failures, input validation errors, business logic errors) are reported in tool results with isError: true.

q.en: A client library parses a tools/list cursor string, assumes it is a base ten offset, and increments it locally instead of sending back exactly what the server issued. Why is this design fragile under 2026-07-28?

o.en: Because an incremented cursor is always immediately rejected outright with a -32601 method not found error every single time
Because a cursor is opaque and server chosen, so reinterpreting it breaks the moment the server changes page size
Because cursors stay valid for exactly one minute after being issued, regardless of how they are used
Because pagination was replaced entirely by cacheScope in this particular revision, and cursors simply no longer exist

x.en: Pagination cursors are opaque by design specifically so the server retains freedom over page size and internal ordering. A client that parses and reconstructs a cursor is relying on an implementation detail that can silently break with any server-side change, which is exactly what opacity is meant to prevent.

questions.setTitle: MCPA Full-Length Mock 3: Design and Security Trade-offs

cite.text: The cursor is an opaque string token, representing a position in the result set - Page size is determined by the server, and clients MUST NOT assume a fixed page size

q.en: A server needs to end a subscriptions/listen stream in two different situations: a graceful, planned end of the subscription, and an abrupt teardown the server initiates. What is the correct message for each case?

o.en: A graceful end always uses a fresh tools/call, and a teardown always uses server/discover instead
Both cases always use the exact same notifications/cancelled message, since the client cannot ever tell the difference
A graceful end answers the listen request with a complete result, while notifications/cancelled tears the stream down
Both cases require the client to reopen a brand new HTTP connection before either message sends

x.en: The specification treats a graceful end and a server-initiated teardown as distinct: a graceful close answers the original listen request with a complete result carrying the subscription id, while notifications/cancelled is the message reserved specifically for the server tearing a listen stream down.

questions.setTitle: MCPA Full-Length Mock 3: Design and Security Trade-offs

cite.text: The client cancels it — close the SSE stream (HTTP) or send `notifications/cancelled` referencing the `subscriptions/listen` request ID (stdio). - The server tears it down (e.g., during shutdown) — it SHOULD send a successful `subscriptions/listen` response to signal a graceful end (see Graceful Closure), then close the stream. - The underlying transport closes (HTTP timeout, TCP disconnect, stdio process exit).

q.en: A destructive tool call times out with no response, and its server-reported idempotentHint is false. Since annotations are self reported and untrusted unless the server itself is trusted, what should the client's retry design do?

o.en: Retry only after first fully switching the entire connection over to stdio, since stdio never produces any ambiguous timeouts at all
Retry immediately and automatically with a new id, trusting the reported hint to mean it is safe
Ignore the timeout entirely and wait forever rather than making any decision about it at all
Treat the outcome as unknown and require explicit confirmation before reissuing a call whose effect could not be observed

x.en: Because idempotentHint is an untrusted, self reported hint from a server that may not be trusted, a client cannot safely assume a timed out destructive call is either done or safe to repeat. The prudent design treats the outcome as unknown and requires explicit confirmation before retrying.

questions.setTitle: MCPA Full-Length Mock 3: Design and Security Trade-offs

q.en: A tool's description field contains text instructing the model to also call a different, unrelated server's delete_account tool whenever this tool is used. What is the correct trust-boundary response to this discovery?

o.en: Treat the tool description as untrusted content, refuse to let it steer a call into another server, and flag it for review
Forward the instruction straight to the model without any comment at all, since the model must filter unsafe text entirely on its own
Delete the entire tool registry for every connected server, since one bad description proves all are compromised
Trust the instruction fully, since any text inside a tool definition is implicitly approved already by the operator

x.en: Tool descriptions, like other server-authored content, are untrusted input to the model and can carry tool poisoning or cross-server steering attempts. The correct design quarantines the instruction rather than acting on it, and treats a server that ships one as a candidate for review, not blanket distrust of every server.

questions.setTitle: MCPA Full-Length Mock 3: Design and Security Trade-offs

cite.text: In particular, descriptions of tool behavior such as annotations should be considered untrusted, unless obtained from a trusted server.

q.en: A resources/read result returns document text that includes an embedded instruction telling the model to ignore its current task and export credentials. Which trust zone is responsible for making sure that instruction never reaches the model as if it were trustworthy guidance?

o.en: The model itself, since it alone stays fully responsible for recognizing every single injection attempt entirely unaided
The host and client, since they own labeling and sanitizing untrusted content before it enters model context
The authorization server, since OAuth scopes are what prevent embedded instructions from ever being read
The upstream document's original author, since the host has no ability to inspect resource content at all

x.en: Resource contents are untrusted input the same as tool results, and the host and client are the trust zone positioned to label and sanitize such content before it becomes part of the model's context, rather than leaving detection entirely to the model or to unrelated infrastructure like the authorization server.

questions.setTitle: MCPA Full-Length Mock 3: Design and Security Trade-offs

q.en: A client team notices its authorization server ignores the RFC 8707 resource parameter and proposes dropping it from the authorization and token requests to simplify the code. What is the correct design decision?

o.en: Replace it with a custom audience header, since servers read audience from headers
Drop it from the token request only, since audience is fixed at authorization time
Keep sending it on both requests, since MCP clients must send it whether or not it is supported
Drop it, since a parameter the authorization server ignores cannot affect security at all

x.en: MCP clients must send the resource parameter, naming the canonical server URI, on both the authorization and token requests regardless of whether the authorization server supports it. It is what lets a supporting authorization server bind a token's audience to one MCP server, so dropping it silently weakens the deployment the day the authorization server starts honoring it.

questions.setTitle: MCPA Full-Length Mock 3: Design and Security Trade-offs

cite.text: MCP clients MUST include the `resource` parameter in authorization and token requests as specified in the Resource Parameter Implementation section

q.en: An MCP server needs to call a third-party API on the user's behalf. One design passes the user's incoming bearer token straight through to that API; another design has the server obtain and use a separate token scoped to that API. Which design is correct, and why?

o.en: Pass the incoming token through, but only when the API happens to be owned by the same company
Cache the incoming token locally and openly replay it to every downstream system the tool ever needs to reach at all times
Pass the incoming token through, since reusing one token everywhere is simpler for the user to reason about
Obtain a separate token for the API, since passthrough is forbidden and a server must validate any token it accepts

x.en: Token passthrough is explicitly forbidden because a token issued for the MCP server was never validated as intended for the downstream API, creating a confused deputy risk. The server must validate audience for tokens it accepts and obtain its own, separately scoped token for any upstream call it makes.

questions.setTitle: MCPA Full-Length Mock 3: Design and Security Trade-offs

cite.text: "Token passthrough" is an anti-pattern where an MCP server accepts tokens from an MCP client without validating that the tokens were properly issued _to the MCP server_ and passes them through to the downstream API.

q.en: A gateway operator proposes forwarding the single incoming bearer token unchanged to every downstream MCP server behind the gateway, arguing it removes the need to manage per-server credentials. What is the flaw in this design?

o.en: It lets a token issued for one audience reach servers it was never validated against, which passthrough forbids
It only ever really fails when the gateway uses Streamable HTTP rather than stdio to reach far downstream servers anyway every time
It is flawless, since a bearer token by definition already grants unlimited access to any receiver
It is unnecessary to avoid, since audience validation was removed from the specification in this revision

x.en: A single forwarded token is a textbook token passthrough problem: each downstream server must validate that a token was issued for it, and a token minted for the gateway or for one server was never vetted for another. The gateway needs to mint or exchange distinct, audience-scoped tokens per server instead.

questions.setTitle: MCPA Full-Length Mock 3: Design and Security Trade-offs

cite.text: Audience. Your MCP server must reject tokens that weren't issued for it. The `resource` value from the client should become the token's audience, which is the `aud` claim in a JWT. Some products need a setting for this, or let you configure the audience on a scope instead. Others always use their own identifier. In that case, compare the audience with that identifier, and keep your server's URL as the PRM `resource`. The identifier must belong to this MCP server only, so don't share one application registration between servers.

q.en: A host is deciding whether to rely on a tool's title and description text to reassure the user before a destructive call, or to run an explicit MRTR elicitation asking the user to confirm. Which design is more defensible, given annotations are untrusted hints?

o.en: Neither, since destructive tools should simply never ever be safely callable under any circumstances at all here whatsoever
Explicit elicitation, since it produces a real user decision the host controls, rather than trusting server-authored text
The description text alone, but only for tools whose name happens to contain the word safe
The description text alone, since a well written description is functionally equivalent to asking the user

x.en: Because tool titles and descriptions are server authored and untrusted unless the server itself is trusted, they cannot substitute for a real consent decision. An MRTR elicitation round trip is the mechanism that gets an explicit answer from the user rather than assuming reassurance from text the server controls.

questions.setTitle: MCPA Full-Length Mock 3: Design and Security Trade-offs

cite.text: Tool Safety - Tools represent arbitrary code execution and must be treated with appropriate caution. - In particular, descriptions of tool behavior such as annotations should be considered untrusted, unless obtained from a trusted server. - Hosts must obtain explicit user consent before invoking any tool - Users should understand what each tool does before authorizing its use

q.en: A deploy tool uses MRTR elicitation to collect a human approval before running, and the pending decision is carried in requestState. Select the three protections that requestState needs given it is attacker-controlled input.

o.en: Binding to the authenticated principal so one user's pending approval cannot be replayed by another
Integrity protection such as an HMAC or AEAD so it cannot be modified undetected
A short expiry combined with single-use enforcement on the server so it cannot be replayed later
A cacheScope of public so the pending approval can be shared efficiently across every user

x.en: Because requestState is round tripped through the client and is not itself trusted, it needs integrity protection, principal binding, and a short, single-use expiry enforced server side. A public cacheScope is unrelated and actively wrong here, since MRTR results including input_required are never cached at all.

questions.setTitle: MCPA Full-Length Mock 3: Design and Security Trade-offs

cite.text: the authenticated principal, rejecting state presented by a different principal.

q.en: An audit pipeline is being designed to record who performed a sensitive tool call. One proposal attributes the action using the self reported clientInfo.name from the request; another uses the authenticated principal derived from the validated access token. Which is correct?

o.en: clientInfo.name, since it is the field explicitly designed for identifying a caller in an audit trail
Whichever field simply happens to be shorter, since shorter values keep audit records far more compact over a long time
The authenticated principal from the token, since clientInfo is self reported and meant only for display and debugging
Both fields combined with an OR, so either one alone counts as sufficient proof of identity

x.en: clientInfo and serverInfo are explicitly self reported and meant only for display, logging, and debugging, never for security decisions. An audit trail that must actually attribute an action correctly needs the authenticated principal established through token validation, not a value the caller could freely set.

questions.setTitle: MCPA Full-Length Mock 3: Design and Security Trade-offs

cite.text: `io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo` and `io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo` are self-reported by the sender and are not verified by the protocol. They are intended for display, logging, and debugging. Implementations SHOULD NOT use them to change the behavior of the client or server, and SHOULD NOT rely on them for security decisions.

q.en: Which two statements correctly describe the client registration priority order for 2026-07-28? Select two.

o.en: Dynamic Client Registration is checked before Client ID Metadata Documents whenever both are advertised
Pre-registered credentials are tried first, ahead of any dynamic or document-based registration mechanism
Asking the user is the fallback of last resort, used only once the automated options are unavailable
Client ID Metadata Documents may only be used by clients that also support the deprecated Dynamic Client Registration flow

x.en: The order is pre-registered credentials first, then Client ID Metadata Documents when advertised, then the deprecated Dynamic Client Registration, and finally asking the user as a last resort. CIMD does not require DCR support, and DCR is checked after CIMD, not before it.

questions.setTitle: MCPA Full-Length Mock 3: Design and Security Trade-offs

cite.text: Dynamic Client Registration (DCR) is deprecated as of protocol version `2026-07-28`. New implementations should use Client ID Metadata Documents (CIMD) instead.

q.en: A registry-listed server silently changes a tool's description and inputSchema between two releases, in a way that expands what the tool actually does. What control design catches this kind of rug pull before the new behavior reaches production?

o.en: Waiting patiently for a user complaint, since definition changes are always noticeable immediately during normal daily use
Trusting the registry's namespace verification alone, since a verified namespace also guarantees definitions never change
Disabling the tool permanently the first time it is ever called, regardless of whether anything changed
Pinning tool definitions by hash and holding any changed definition for review before it is trusted again

x.en: Registry namespace verification proves who owns a name, not that its tool definitions stay the same over time, so definition drift needs its own control: pinning a known-good definition by hash and flagging any change for review before the updated tool is trusted in production.

questions.setTitle: MCPA Full-Length Mock 3: Design and Security Trade-offs

q.en: A host has two servers connected, A and B. A tool result from server A contains text asking the host to immediately call an administrative tool on server B. What is the correct trust design?

o.en: Treat server A's content as untrusted with respect to server B, and never let one server's output authorize a call into another
Allow it, since both servers were separately approved by the same administrator and therefore trust each other
Allow it only if server A's very own tool has readOnlyHint explicitly and clearly set to true in its own listed annotations somewhere
Allow it, since the host's only job is to relay whatever a connected server's result requests

x.en: Trust boundaries are per server, not transitive across servers just because a host happens to be connected to both. Content returned by one server must never be treated as authorization to act on a different server, since that would let any single compromised or careless server steer the entire host.

questions.setTitle: MCPA Full-Length Mock 3: Design and Security Trade-offs

q.en: Which two design elements make an audit and trace system useful for reviewing an incident that crossed a host, a client, and two servers? Select two.

o.en: Writing tamper-evident, for example hash-chained, records so a reviewer can detect whether a log entry was altered after the fact
Propagating OpenTelemetry trace context such as traceparent through _meta so spans across hops can be correlated
Recording only the final aggregate outcome of the entire multi-hop exchange, discarding intermediate steps to save storage
Letting each hop choose its own unrelated identifier scheme so operators can compare formats after the fact

x.en: Correlating activity across hops needs a shared trace context propagated end to end, and reviewing an incident needs confidence that the records themselves were not altered, which tamper evidence provides. Discarding intermediate steps or letting each hop invent its own identifiers both destroy the correlation an audit needs.

questions.setTitle: MCPA Full-Length Mock 3: Design and Security Trade-offs

q.en: A team proposes setting cacheScope to public on a resource that contains per-tenant billing data, reasoning that a public cache reduces load and every tenant's client already has a valid token. What is wrong with this design?

o.en: Nothing is wrong, since holding a valid token is by itself sufficient proof cacheScope public is safe
cacheScope public would let one tenant's cached response be served to a different tenant, since it governs sharing, not access
cacheScope only ever really affects tools/list results specifically, so it has no real bearing on resources/read at all here whatsoever
The only fix needed is to shorten ttlMs, since a shorter freshness window makes any scope safe

x.en: cacheScope public means a result may be shared across users and tokens, which is precisely wrong for per-tenant billing data even though every caller holds a valid token. Because cacheScope is never an access control mechanism, per-tenant data needs private scope and its own per-read authorization check, not a shorter TTL.

questions.setTitle: MCPA Full-Length Mock 3: Design and Security Trade-offs

cite.text: A `cacheScope` of `"public"` indicates that the response does not contain user-specific data and can be safely shared. Servers MUST be aware that responses with a `"public"` `cacheScope` may be shared between callers even if the Result is coming from an authenticated endpoint. For example, the Result from an authenticated `tools/list` call with a `"public"` `cacheScope` may be cached by a client and may be shared outside of the initial request's authorization context (i.e. different access tokens can leverage the same cache).

q.en: A client stored registration credentials after successfully registering with authorization server A. It now needs to connect to a different authorization server B for a separate deployment, and B also supports the same registration mechanism. What is the correct design?

o.en: Reuse the credentials stored for server A directly with server B right away, since one successful registration should cover every future authorization server encountered
Wait patiently for server A to forward the stored credentials to server B fully automatically before any single request to B is ever attempted at all
Register separately with server B and keep credentials keyed by issuer, since persisted credentials must never be reused across a different authorization server
Ask the user to manually paste server A's credentials into server B's configuration screen so both servers share one identity

x.en: Registration state is bound to the authorization server that issued it. Persisted credentials must be keyed by issuer, and a client must register again, rather than reuse or transfer them, whenever it connects to a different authorization server, even one that supports the same registration mechanism.

questions.setTitle: MCPA Full-Length Mock 3: Design and Security Trade-offs

cite.text: Clients that use pre-registered credentials, or persist client credentials obtained via Dynamic Client Registration, MUST associate those credentials with the specific authorization server that issued them, keyed by the authorization server's `issuer` identifier. When the authorization server changes (detected via updated protected resource metadata), clients MUST NOT reuse client credentials from a different authorization server and MUST re-register with the new authorization server.

q.en: A team wants a reusable, user-invoked, slash-command-style template with arguments that a person deliberately selects to start a code review conversation. Which primitive fits this control model, and why not the alternatives?

o.en: A resource, since resources are application-driven content the host attaches without the user choosing it each time
A tool, since tools are always model-controlled and the model alone would decide on its own when to invoke it
Server instructions returned from server/discover, since those are supposedly the only user-facing text a server could ever expose to anyone
A prompt, since prompts are user-controlled templates a person deliberately selects, matching how this template is meant to be used

x.en: The three server primitives map to three different control models: tools are model-controlled, resources are application-driven, and prompts are user-controlled templates a person explicitly selects. A deliberately chosen, argument-taking template for starting a conversation is exactly the user-controlled case prompts were designed for.

questions.setTitle: MCPA Full-Length Mock 3: Design and Security Trade-offs

cite.text: Prompts are designed to be user-controlled, meaning they are exposed from servers to clients with the intention of the user being able to explicitly select them for use. This refers to who decides when the prompt is used, not who authors its content. Prompt content is defined by the server.

q.en: A tool is meant to be called only by an app's own embedded UI, to refresh its view, and should never appear as something the model can invoke on its own. Under the MCP Apps extension, how should the tool's _meta.ui visibility be set, and what must the host do as a result?

o.en: Set visibility to only app, and the host must not list the tool to the model while still letting the app call it
Set visibility to only app, but the host stays free to list it to the model anyway
Set visibility to only model instead, since visibility supposedly only ever controls what the human user is ever allowed to see at all
Leave visibility completely unset, since every tool is always callable by both the model and the app equally anyway

x.en: MCP Apps lets a tool restrict who may invoke it: when visibility excludes model, the host must not list that tool to the agent, and when it excludes app, the host must reject a tools/call coming from the rendered UI. An app-only refresh action should declare app so only the embedded interface can trigger it.

questions.setTitle: MCPA Full-Length Mock 3: Design and Security Trade-offs

q.en: A vendor markets a brand new SDK as fully spec-compliant and ready to use, but it currently sits at Tier 3 in the official tiering system. Before recommending it for a customer's production deployment, what should an integrator conclude from that tier alone?

o.en: That it ships absolutely every official extension by default, since extension support is apparently mandatory at every single tier without exception
That it is explicitly experimental, with no guaranteed conformance percentage or timeline the way Tier 1 and 2 commit to
That it already passes one hundred percent of conformance tests, since every vendor SDK starts out at Tier 1 by default
That it will automatically and fully graduate to Tier 1 within just two business days of the vendor's claim

x.en: SDK tiers describe real, graduated commitments: Tier 1 passes all conformance tests with fast triage, Tier 2 passes most within a longer window, and Tier 3 is explicitly experimental with none of those guarantees. A vendor's marketing claim of spec compliance does not override what the tier itself actually commits to.

questions.setTitle: MCPA Full-Length Mock 3: Design and Security Trade-offs

cite.text: Tier 1 SDKs are fully supported and implement every non-experimental feature, including optional capabilities such as sampling and elicitation. SDKs in Tier 2 are actively maintained and working toward full specification support, and those in Tier 3 are experimental, partially implemented, or specialized. Experimental features and protocol extensions (such as Tasks and MCP Apps) are not required for any tier.

q.en: In a gateway-fronted enterprise deployment over Streamable HTTP, whose responsibility is validating the Origin header and binding to localhost when appropriate? What goes wrong if that responsibility is assumed to belong to someone else?

o.en: The end user's, since only a human can decide whether a request's origin looks legitimate
The registry publisher's, since server.json is where Origin policy is supposed to be declared
The server or gateway operator's, and if neither implements it, the deployment is open to DNS rebinding attacks
Nobody's at all really, since Origin validation only ever matters for stdio transports and never at all for Streamable HTTP

x.en: Origin validation and localhost binding are HTTP transport security controls that the server or the gateway sitting in front of it must actually implement. If each side assumes the other handles it, the deployment ends up with no real defense against the DNS rebinding style attacks that control was meant to stop.

questions.setTitle: MCPA Full-Length Mock 3: Design and Security Trade-offs

cite.text: Servers MUST validate the `Origin` header on all incoming connections to prevent DNS rebinding attacks. - If the `Origin` header is present and invalid, servers MUST respond with HTTP 403 Forbidden. The HTTP response body MAY comprise a JSON-RPC _error response_ that has no `id`. 2. When running locally, servers SHOULD bind only to localhost (127.0.0.1) rather than all network interfaces (0.0.0.0). 3. Servers SHOULD implement proper authentication for all connections.

q.en: A nightly batch job runs unattended, calling a server with no user present and no elicitation capability declared. It needs the equivalent of long running work tracking. Which design fits, and why would MRTR elicitation be the wrong choice here?

o.en: Dynamic Client Registration, since machine clients must always dynamically register again before every single batch run without exception
A plain synchronous call held open for the job's entire duration, since batch jobs are typically always expected to block
MRTR elicitation, since a server can always request user input from a client even with nobody watching
The tasks extension or a server-minted handle, since elicitation needs a client capability an unattended job will not declare

x.en: MRTR input requests such as elicitation assume a capability the client declares and a way to gather an answer, neither of which fits an unattended machine-to-machine job with nobody present. Tracking long, unattended work instead fits the tasks extension or an explicit server-minted handle referenced on later calls.

questions.setTitle: MCPA Full-Length Mock 3: Design and Security Trade-offs

q.en: A registry lists a server under a reverse-DNS namespace that has already passed GitHub ownership verification. A reviewer treats that verification alone as proof the server's published code is safe to run. What is the flaw in that conclusion?

o.en: Namespace verification proves who controls the name, not that the code is safe, since scanning is delegated to package registries and aggregators
There is truly no flaw at all, since GitHub ownership verification already includes a full independent security audit of the published code itself
The flaw is that GitHub verification technically only ever applies to DNS challenges, never to namespace ownership claims themselves at all
The flaw is that reverse-DNS namespaces were entirely removed from the registry design as of this specification revision

x.en: Namespace verification through GitHub, DNS, or an HTTP challenge establishes ownership of a name, which stops impersonation, but the registry explicitly delegates security scanning to package registries and aggregators, so ownership proof alone says nothing about whether the published code itself is safe to run.

questions.setTitle: MCPA Full-Length Mock 3: Design and Security Trade-offs

cite.text: With any authentication method, the Registry verifies that you control the namespace in `name`; it does not verify that you control the remote URL. See Ownership Verification for details.

q.en: Select the three facts about SDK tiers that should shape a build-versus-adopt decision for a client library.

o.en: A Tier 1 SDK commits to triaging issues within two business days and fixing critical bugs within seven
Extensions are not a requirement at any SDK tier, so their absence does not by itself indicate a lower tier
Tier 3 SDKs are always required to support every single official extension before they can ever be published
An SDK can be relegated to a lower tier after four consecutive weeks of conformance failures

x.en: Tier 1 commitments, the relegation rule after sustained failures, and the fact that extensions are optional at every tier are all real signals for a build-versus-adopt call. No tier mandates supporting every official extension, so that claim is false and would mislead a team using extension coverage to judge tier.

questions.setTitle: MCPA Full-Length Mock 3: Design and Security Trade-offs

cite.text: Resolve security and critical bugs within seven days

q.en: A server exposes several skills through Skills over MCP. A client calls resources/read on one skill's SKILL.md file just to preview its contents. Has that skill been activated by this read?

o.en: No, since Skills over MCP never permits resources/read to return SKILL.md content at all
No, reading the file through resources/read makes it merely readable, a step distinct from activation
Yes, reading SKILL.md through resources/read is what activation means under this extension by definition
Yes, but only for skills whose description field happens to be under one hundred characters

x.en: Reading a skill's SKILL.md through resources/read only retrieves text. Skills over MCP treats skill content as untrusted input, leaves whether a skill is loaded into model context to explicit user policy, and has hosts let users inspect a skill before loading it, so previewing a file is not activation.

questions.setTitle: MCPA Full-Length Mock 3: Design and Security Trade-offs

cite.text: Reading `SKILL.md` through `resources/read` does not itself activate a skill. To load the skill, the host routes the read through its skill-loading path, which verifies the content and applies any required user approval before loading it into model context.

q.en: A client was built and tested only against one specific MCP server. Under 2026-07-28, why should that same client generally be able to work against a different, unrelated, modern server without code changes?

o.en: Because every MCP server is legally required to expose an identical set of tool names
Because servers share a single global process and therefore already know about every client in advance
Because a compliant client relies on discovery and the wire protocol rather than one server's internal assumptions
Because the client's own author is always expected to hardcode that one specific server's tool names directly into the client itself

x.en: Portability follows directly from where logic is supposed to live: a client that discovers capabilities and tools through the protocol, rather than hardcoding one server's specifics, can drive any compliant server it has never seen. Custom, server-specific assumptions baked into a client are exactly what breaks that portability.

questions.setTitle: MCPA Full-Length Mock 3: Design and Security Trade-offs

q.en: A platform team is deciding whether a new extension can be turned on for every user by default the moment a vendor SDK adds support for it. What does the specification's extension design actually require here?

o.en: The host must wait for the extension's identifier to change to a -v2 suffix before enabling it
Nothing further at all, since any extension a client's own SDK supports is automatically enabled for every single request
The extension must first be promoted from Tier 3 to Tier 1 before it can ever be declared
Explicit opt-in on both sides, since extensions are disabled by default, which is where governance sign-off belongs

x.en: Extensions are disabled by default and require explicit opt-in through declared capabilities on both the client and server side, which is a deliberate design choice, not an accident of SDK support. That deliberate opt-in point is precisely where a platform team's governance review naturally fits before wide rollout.

questions.setTitle: MCPA Full-Length Mock 3: Design and Security Trade-offs

cite.text: SDKs MAY implement extensions. Where implemented, extensions MUST be disabled by default and require explicit opt-in. SDK documentation SHOULD list supported extensions.

q.en: A developer is deciding whether to expose a purely internal helper function, called only within the same process and never crossing an application or trust boundary, as an MCP tool. Is this a good fit for MCP?

o.en: No, since MCP is built for crossing the boundary between an application and an external system, and this helper never crosses it
No, but only because internal helper functions are always too fast for JSON-RPC to keep up with
Yes, since any function at all becomes more valuable once it is exposed through a protocol
Yes, since MCP technically always requires every single function anywhere in a codebase to eventually always be reachable as a tool too

x.en: MCP exists to standardize context and actions crossing the boundary between an AI application and an external system. A same-process internal helper never crosses that boundary, so wrapping it as a tool adds serialization and discovery overhead without the interoperability benefit that justifies using the protocol in the first place.

questions.setTitle: MCPA Full-Length Mock 3: Design and Security Trade-offs

q.en: A gateway operator wants to cache a server's public server/discover result across every tenant to cut latency. Is sharing that cached result across tenants consistent with the caching contract, and what must the gateway still keep separate?

o.en: It is consistent, and caching the discover result is by itself sufficient to authorize every tenant's requests
It is consistent, and per-tenant authorization must still be enforced on every actual request regardless of what was cached
It is inconsistent, since server/discover results can never ever carry a cacheScope of public under any circumstances at all
It is inconsistent, since sharing any cached value across tenants is forbidden no matter what scope declares

x.en: server/discover is one of the results that carries ttlMs and cacheScope, and a public discover result, capability metadata rather than tenant-specific data, is a reasonable candidate for shared caching. That caching decision is still separate from authorization, which the gateway must keep enforcing per tenant on every later request.

questions.setTitle: MCPA Full-Length Mock 3: Design and Security Trade-offs

cite.text: A `cacheScope` of `"public"` indicates that the response does not contain user-specific data and can be safely shared. Servers MUST be aware that responses with a `"public"` `cacheScope` may be shared between callers even if the Result is coming from an authenticated endpoint. For example, the Result from an authenticated `tools/list` call with a `"public"` `cacheScope` may be cached by a client and may be shared outside of the initial request's authorization context (i.e. different access tokens can leverage the same cache).

q.en: What does a domain's weight in the MCPA blueprint most directly tell a candidate?

o.en: The order in which the five domains appear in the official guide
The share of exam questions drawn from that domain, on average
The minimum score a candidate must reach in that domain alone
The number of official training hours required before attempting it

x.en: A domain's published weight is its share of the blueprint, the proportion of exam content the domain represents; it does not set a reading order, a required hour count, or a per-domain minimum score.

questions.setTitle: The MCPA Blueprint Is a Study Budget, Not a Checklist

q.en: Which pair of domains carries the largest combined share of the MCPA blueprint?

o.en: MCP Fundamentals and Architecture and Components, the two foundational domains
Architecture and Components and Use Cases and Ecosystem, the two mid-weight domains
Interactions and Execution and Security and Governance, the two heaviest domains
Use Cases and Ecosystem and MCP Fundamentals, the two adoption-facing domains

x.en: Interactions and Execution is weighted 26 percent and Security and Governance is weighted 24 percent, together half the blueprint, which is why they deserve the largest share of study hours.

questions.setTitle: The MCPA Blueprint Is a Study Budget, Not a Checklist

q.en: The MCPA certification page and the Linux Foundation's own launch press release disagree about one exam fact. Which fact is it, and which source does this curriculum follow?

o.en: The included retake count
The credential validity period
The exam fee
The exam duration

x.en: The certification page states a 90 minute duration while the press release states 120 minutes; this curriculum follows the certification page as the exam-specific source and records the conflict rather than silently choosing a number.

questions.setTitle: The MCPA Blueprint Is a Study Budget, Not a Checklist

review.note: Domanda sul curriculum, non sull'esame. La discrepanza è risolta: le pagine LF attuali indicano 90 minuti. / About the curriculum, not the exam: current LF pages state 90 minutes.

q.en: A practice question claims a client must call initialize before a 2026-07-28 server will accept any other request. How should a prepared candidate read that claim?

o.en: A legacy-era protocol distractor
True only for older MCP servers
A detail specific to stdio only
A true, still current requirement

x.en: The 2026-07-28 revision removed the initialize handshake and protocol sessions entirely, so every request now carries its own protocol version and capabilities in its metadata instead of relying on a prior handshake.

questions.setTitle: The MCPA Blueprint Is a Study Budget, Not a Checklist

q.en: A candidate scores 100 percent in MCP Fundamentals, weighted 16 percent, and 0 percent everywhere else. Why is a weighted readiness estimate more useful here than a plain five-way average?

o.en: It rounds every domain score upward so the candidate always looks prepared
It shows readiness near 16 percent instead of a misleading 20 percent average
It replaces the five domains with a single combined pass or fail flag
It discards the weakest domain scores before computing any final result

x.en: A plain average shows 20 percent because one of five domains is perfect, but a weighted estimate reflects that the mastered domain is only 16 percent of the exam, which is a more honest picture of overall readiness.

questions.setTitle: The MCPA Blueprint Is a Study Budget, Not a Checklist

q.en: A few lessons in the 34-lesson route, such as JSON-RPC and Meta, are tagged with two domains instead of one. What does that reflect about the route?

o.en: A sign those lessons are optional to skip
A sign those lessons get double the study time
A concept tested from two domains at once
A numbering error the curriculum needs to fix

x.en: A lesson can sit at a genuine intersection, such as a message envelope that is both a core concept and a piece of the architecture, so the route tags it under both domains rather than forcing one arbitrary choice.

questions.setTitle: The MCPA Blueprint Is a Study Budget, Not a Checklist

q.en: According to the specification overview, which three components MUST every MCP implementation support?

o.en: Server features, client features, and utilities
Resources, prompts, tools, and elicitation together
The base protocol, versioning, and message patterns
Authorization, extensions, and completion utilities

x.en: The specification states that all implementations MUST support the base protocol, versioning, and the message patterns, while server features, client features, authorization, and utilities MAY be implemented as the application needs them.

cite.text: All implementations MUST support the base protocol, versioning, and the message patterns. Other components MAY be implemented based on the specific needs of the application.

q.en: A sentence reads, written in lowercase, that a client must not batch requests. What normative weight does that carry under BCP 14?

o.en: The same forbidding weight as MUST NOT written in capitals
It makes that whole paragraph an invalid specification page
A soft recommendation, treated the same as SHOULD NOT
No normative weight; only capitalized keywords count

x.en: BCP 14 keywords carry their defined meaning only when they appear in all capitals; the identical words in lowercase are ordinary prose with no normative force.

cite.text: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 [RFC2119] [RFC8174] when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

q.en: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between schema.ts and schema.json in the specification repository?

o.en: schema.ts is the source of truth and schema.json is generated from it
schema.json is authoritative for SDKs and schema.ts is only a draft
schema.json is written by hand first and schema.ts is generated from it
The two files are maintained independently and are free to disagree

x.en: The specification names schema.ts the source of truth for every protocol message and structure, with schema.json generated automatically from it for tooling.

cite.text: There is also a JSON Schema, which is automatically generated from the TypeScript source of truth, for use with various automated tooling.

q.en: A feature is marked Deprecated in the specification revision released on 2026-07-28 with a twelve-month window. From what point is that window measured?

o.en: From the day the Core Maintainers approved the SEP in review
From the release of the specification revision that marks it Deprecated
From the day the deprecation SEP itself reached Final status
From the day the deprecation SEP was first opened as a pull request

x.en: SEP-2596 measures the deprecation window from the release of the revision that first marks the feature Deprecated, not from whenever its own SEP happened to reach Final.

cite.text: When the deprecation SEP reaches Final the deprecation is scheduled: the following changes land in the draft specification (`schema/draft/` and `docs/specification/draft/`). The feature becomes Deprecated when the revision carrying these changes is released as Current under the [versioning guide][versioning], and the minimum deprecation window is counted from that release. Anchoring the clock to the revision release means every feature deprecated in the same revision shares one earliest removal rather than each carrying a date derived from when its own SEP happened to land.

q.en: Roots, Sampling, and Logging are sometimes described as having been removed in the 2026-07-28 revision. What does the specification actually say about their state?

o.en: Active still; nothing about their status changed in this revision
Removed outright; a conformant server MUST NOT implement them
Deprecated, not removed; still fully specified and functional
Experimental now; only Tier 3 SDKs are required to support them

x.en: SEP-2577 deprecated Roots, Sampling, and Logging in the 2026-07-28 revision; they remain fully specified and functional, with removal not eligible before the first revision released on or after 2027-07-28.

cite.text: Deprecated: The Sampling feature is deprecated as of protocol version `2026-07-28` (SEP-2577). Under the feature lifecycle policy, it remains in the specification for at least twelve months after this revision's release before it becomes eligible for removal. New implementations SHOULD NOT adopt it; existing implementations SHOULD migrate to integrating directly with LLM provider APIs. See the deprecated features registry.

q.en: A changelog entry cites a SEP number as the source of a major protocol change. What should a careful reader do before repeating that claim?

o.en: Assume the change is still in review until the next revision ships
Read only the schema.json diff, since SEPs rarely touch the schema
Trust the one-line changelog summary, since SEPs close once accepted
Open the SEP file for its text, rationale, and final status

x.en: A changelog entry links back to the SEP that produced it, and reading the SEP itself confirms the exact specification text, the rationale, and whether it actually reached Final status.

q.en: Four AI applications each need to reach six external systems. How many implementations does one shared protocol require?

o.en: Six, because only the external systems implement anything at all
Four, because only the AI applications implement anything at all
Ten, because each application and each system implements it once
Twenty-four, because each pair still needs its own custom glue

x.en: A shared protocol turns N times M pairings into N plus M implementations: four clients plus six servers is ten.

cite.text: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open-source standard for connecting AI applications to external systems.

q.en: In the 2026-07-28 revision, how does a server learn which protocol version a request uses?

o.en: From the version the server advertised in its latest tools/list reply
From the initialize handshake that opened the connection earlier on
From a session identifier the server assigned on the first request
From io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion in the request's _meta

x.en: The protocol is stateless: every request carries its own protocol version and client capabilities in params._meta, with no handshake or session.

cite.text: Make MCP stateless: remove the `initialize`/`notifications/initialized` handshake. Every request now carries its protocol version and client capabilities in `_meta` (`io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion`, `io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities`). Clients SHOULD identify themselves on each request (`io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo`), and servers SHOULD identify themselves in each result's `_meta` (`io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo`). Version mismatches return `UnsupportedProtocolVersionError` (SEP-2575).

q.en: A client sends tools/call naming a tool the server does not expose. What does a conformant server return?

o.en: A JSON-RPC error with code -32602 because the params are invalid
An input_required result asking the user to pick a different tool
A JSON-RPC error with code -32601 because the method is unknown
A normal result with isError set to true and an empty content list

x.en: An unknown tool is a protocol error reported as -32602 Invalid params; -32601 is reserved for an unknown JSON-RPC method.

cite.text: Protocol Errors indicate issues with the request structure itself that models are less likely to be able to fix: Unknown tool; Malformed requests; Server errors. They are returned as standard JSON-RPC errors (example: code -32602, "Unknown tool: invalid_tool_name").

q.en: Which statement correctly describes who controls each server primitive?

o.en: All three primitives are chosen by the server operator ahead of time
Tools are model-controlled, resources app-driven, prompts user-controlled
Tools are user-controlled, resources model-controlled, prompts app-driven
All three primitives are chosen by the model at runtime without the host

x.en: The model decides when to invoke tools, the host application decides which resources enter context, and the user explicitly selects prompts.

cite.text: Tools in MCP are designed to be model-controlled, meaning that the language model can discover and invoke tools automatically based on its contextual understanding and the user's prompts.

q.en: A call to get_forecast omits its required city argument. Which response best helps the model recover?

o.en: An empty successful result so that the conversation keeps going
A JSON-RPC error -32603 that reports an internal server failure
A result with isError true that explains the city is required
A JSON-RPC error -32602 that the host withholds from the model

x.en: Input problems are tool execution errors: a normal result with isError true lets the model read the explanation and retry with a city.

cite.text: Tool Execution Errors contain actionable feedback that language models can use to self-correct and retry with adjusted parameters: API failures; Input validation errors (e.g., date in wrong format, value out of range); Business logic errors. They are reported in tool results with isError: true.

q.en: Which of these does MCP deliberately leave to the host application instead of standardizing?

o.en: How a server describes the tools it offers to connecting clients
How a client invokes a tool and then reads the result that returns
How results and errors are shaped when they travel on the wire
Which model the host uses and how it assembles its model prompt

x.en: MCP standardizes the conversation between applications and systems; the choice of model and prompt construction remain the host's decisions.

q.en: A raw JSON-RPC message has a method field but no id field at all. Which of the four MCP message shapes is it?

o.en: A request, because every message with a method field is a request
A result response, because the absence of an id means the exchange is already complete
An error response, because errors are the only shape that can omit an id
A notification, since only requests and results are required to carry an id

x.en: A message with a method and no id field at all is a notification; JSON-RPC uses the presence of id to separate a request, which expects a reply, from a notification, which does not.

cite.text: Notifications are sent from the client to the server or vice versa, as a one-way message. The receiver MUST NOT send a response.: Notifications MUST NOT include an ID.

q.en: A 2026-07-28 client receives a result object from a server implementing an earlier protocol version that never sends resultType. How must the client interpret the missing field?

o.en: As complete, the backward-compatible default for servers that predate resultType
As an error, since resultType is mandatory and its absence makes the result malformed
As whichever value the client used in its most recent request
As input_required, since missing information usually blocks completion

x.en: For backward compatibility with servers implementing earlier protocol versions, a client must treat an absent resultType as complete rather than reject the response.

cite.text: For backward compatibility with servers implementing earlier protocol versions, which do not include `resultType`, clients MUST treat an absent `resultType` as `"complete"`.

q.en: Which _meta key prefix is reserved for MCP because its second dot-separated label is modelcontextprotocol or mcp?

o.en: com.example.mcp/, since mcp appears as its third label
dev.mcp/, since its second label is mcp
mcp.example/, since its first label is literally mcp
org.tools.mcp/, since mcp appears at the end of the prefix

x.en: A prefix is reserved for MCP only when its second dot-separated label is modelcontextprotocol or mcp; dev.mcp qualifies because mcp sits in that second position, while the other prefixes place mcp elsewhere.

cite.text: Any prefix where the second label is `modelcontextprotocol` or `mcp` is reserved for MCP use.

q.en: A request's params._meta includes io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion but omits io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities entirely. What must a conformant server do?

o.en: Process the request as if the client declared no optional capabilities
Reject it with JSON-RPC error -32601, since the method itself is now unrecognized
Reject it with JSON-RPC error -32602, and 400 Bad Request on HTTP
Hold the request open until the client sends the missing field in a follow-up

x.en: A request missing a required _meta field such as clientCapabilities is malformed, and a conformant server must reject it with -32602, returning 400 Bad Request on an HTTP transport.

cite.text: A request missing any required field is malformed; the server MUST reject it with JSON-RPC error code `-32602` (Invalid params). On HTTP, the response status MUST be `400 Bad Request`.

q.en: A gateway operator wants to route requests differently depending on which client sent them, reading io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo to decide. Why is that unsafe?

o.en: Only servers may read clientInfo; gateways are restricted to reading _meta.progressToken
The field never reaches the gateway because it is stripped before the request leaves the client
The field is only populated on the first request of a brand-new connection
clientInfo is self-reported by the sender and is never verified by the protocol

x.en: clientInfo and serverInfo are self-reported by whoever sends them and are intended only for display, logging, and debugging, so a routing or authorization decision must never depend on them.

cite.text: `io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo` and `io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo` are self-reported by the sender and are not verified by the protocol. They are intended for display, logging, and debugging. Implementations SHOULD NOT use them to change the behavior of the client or server, and SHOULD NOT rely on them for security decisions.

q.en: A client has three independent requests ready to send to a Streamable HTTP server. What does 2026-07-28 require it to do?

o.en: Send three separate POST requests, one request or notification per body
Join them with newlines in one POST body, one message per line
Open a single SSE stream and push all three requests through it
Combine them into a single JSON-RPC batch array and POST it once

x.en: JSON-RPC batching was removed from MCP in the 2025-06-18 revision, so each Streamable HTTP POST body must carry exactly one request or notification.

cite.text: The body of the HTTP POST MUST be a single JSON-RPC _request_ or _notification_. The client MUST NOT send JSON-RPC _responses_.

q.en: Under MCP 2026-07-28, what must be true of the information a server needs to answer one request?

o.en: It is retrieved from a session record tied to the connection
It builds up gradually across several requests on one connection
It is fully contained in that one single request, nothing inferred
It is cached from the connection's opening handshake exchange

x.en: MCP 2026-07-28 is a stateless protocol: every request is self-describing, and a server must not infer context from requests that arrived earlier, even on the same connection.

cite.text: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a stateless protocol: all the information needed to process a request is contained in the request itself. A server processes each request independently; no state should be inferred from previous requests, even those on the same connection or stream.

q.en: A server just finished handling a client's third request on a long-lived HTTP connection. What may it assume about the fourth request on that same connection?

o.en: The same client capabilities declared earlier still apply to the fourth request
The connection itself now counts as an authenticated session for later requests
The same protocol version negotiated for the third request still applies
Nothing: the fourth request must supply its own version and capabilities again

x.en: Servers must not rely on prior requests over the same connection for capabilities, protocol version, or identity; every request supplies that metadata in its own _meta field.

cite.text: Client requests carry the following `io.modelcontextprotocol/*` fields in `_meta`; fields marked as required MUST be included on every request. Servers use these to identify the protocol version and capabilities in use without relying on any prior connection state. See [Versioning and Compatibility][lifecycle] for version negotiation rules.

q.en: Why does MCP 2026-07-28 make every request self-describing instead of relying on a connection-scoped handshake?

o.en: So any replica can answer it, and a retry is safe to send anywhere
So a server can safely skip validating capabilities on most requests
So a single server process can hold more concurrent connections open
So a client only has to authenticate once per application launch

x.en: Because no state is tied to a specific process, any replica can serve any request, a retry is safe to send to a different replica, and load balancers need no session stickiness.

cite.text: A truly stateless protocol, where every request is self-contained and can be understood in isolation, is highly desirable for its inherent simplicity, scalability, and reliability. The current Model Context Protocol (MCP) is not stateless by default. The specification requires an initialization handshake that establishes a session state between the client and server, which persists for the duration of the connection.

q.en: A client opens one stdio connection and, without closing it, sends a request for user A followed by an unrelated request for user B. What does MCP 2026-07-28 say about this?

o.en: It is fine only if both requests share one authorization token
It is fine; an open connection is never a session or a conversation
It is invalid unless the server issues a new session identifier first
It is invalid; a stdio process may carry only one conversation

x.en: An open connection, such as a stdio process, is not a conversation or session: clients may interleave unrelated requests on the same transport, and a server must not treat connection identity as a proxy for continuity.

cite.text: This implies that an open connection, such as a STDIO process, is not a conversation or session: clients may interleave unrelated requests on the same transport, and a server must not treat connection or process identity as a proxy for conversation or session continuity.

q.en: A server needs a shopping cart to survive across several tool calls. Which design matches SEP-2567 guidance for MCP 2026-07-28?

o.en: Store the cart under the client's connection identifier on the server
Keep the cart in server memory and trust the order requests arrive in
Return an opaque handle from a create tool and reuse it later
Ask the client to resend a session identifier on every cart request

x.en: State that spans multiple requests must be referenced by an explicit identifier the client passes on each request: a server-minted handle returned from a creation tool and threaded through later calls as an ordinary argument.

cite.text: MCP has no protocol-level session, so a server cannot rely on implicit per-connection state to relate one tool call to the next. Servers that need to maintain state across calls — a shopping cart, an open browser context, a database transaction — should do so by returning an explicit handle from a creation tool and accepting that handle as an argument on subsequent calls.

q.en: Which of these did MCP 2026-07-28 remove in order to make statelessness the default?

o.en: The tools/call method and its CallToolResult content list
The per-request _meta field and its protocolVersion value
The server/discover method and its supportedVersions list
The initialize handshake and the Mcp-Session-Id header

x.en: 2026-07-28 removes the initialize handshake, notifications/initialized, and the Mcp-Session-Id header; per-request _meta with protocolVersion, and server/discover, are exactly what replaced them and remain current.

cite.text: This proposal removes the protocol-level session concept from MCP, replacing implicit session-scoped state with explicit, server-minted state handles that the model carries and threads through subsequent calls. [SEP-2575] removes the `initialize` handshake and carries protocol version and capabilities per-request; this proposal is the complementary change that removes sessions and the `Mcp-Session-Id` header. Together they make MCP stateless at the protocol layer.

q.en: Before sending any other request, how does a dual-era client learn whether a stdio MCP server is modern or legacy?

o.en: It assumes every server is modern until a later request happens to fail
It sends a server/discover probe first and reads the shape of the reply
It reads a version banner the server prints to stderr when it launches
It opens two connections and always compares how long each takes to answer

x.en: A dual-era client probes with server/discover before anything else: a DiscoverResult, a recognized modern error, or a non-modern outcome each point to a different era.

questions.setTitle: Telling a Modern MCP Server From a Legacy One

cite.text: Dual-era | Modern | Works. The stdio probe returns a `DiscoverResult` (or `UnsupportedProtocolVersionError`); on HTTP, the first modern request succeeds or returns a modern error. The client stays modern.

q.en: A dual-era client on stdio probes a server and receives a JSON-RPC error with code -32022. What should the client do next?

o.en: Fall back right away to the legacy handshake for that particular server instead
Treat the server as permanently unreachable and stop trying to contact it
Retry the same request using a version the error itself lists as supported
Wait a fixed number of seconds, then repeat the identical request again

x.en: UnsupportedProtocolVersionError is a recognized modern error, so the server is modern: the client retries with a version from data.supported instead of falling back to legacy.

questions.setTitle: Telling a Modern MCP Server From a Legacy One

cite.text: In both cases, a recognized modern JSON-RPC error (such as `UnsupportedProtocolVersionError`) identifies a modern server: the client retries with a supported version rather than falling back. Anything else identifies a legacy server.

q.en: Which outcome of a server/discover probe means the server is modern but speaks a different version than the client asked for?

o.en: An unrecognized error the client has never once seen, with no version data
A DiscoverResult that lists exactly the version the client had requested
No response at all within the client's own configured probe timeout
A recognized version error that also names the versions it does support

x.en: A recognized modern error such as UnsupportedProtocolVersionError still identifies a modern server, just one that needs a different mutually supported version.

questions.setTitle: Telling a Modern MCP Server From a Legacy One

cite.text: The server returns a `DiscoverResult`: the server is modern. Select a mutually supported version from `supportedVersions` and continue. - The server returns a recognized modern JSON-RPC error such as [`UnsupportedProtocolVersionError`][unsupported-version]: the server is modern but does not support the requested version. Use one of the versions in its advertised `supported` list. Do not fall back to `initialize`. - The server returns any other error, or does not respond within a reasonable timeout: the server is legacy. Fall back to the `initialize` handshake.

q.en: On the Streamable HTTP transport, how should a dual-era client decide whether a server that just answered with 400 Bad Request is modern or legacy?

o.en: Read the response body; a recognized modern error still means modern
Treat every 400 response as proof the server only speaks the legacy revision
Retry the exact same unmodified request until the server somehow accepts it
Close the connection and ask whoever configured it to try another server

x.en: Modern servers also answer 400 for version, capability, and header errors, so a dual-era client inspects the body for a recognized modern error before assuming legacy.

questions.setTitle: Telling a Modern MCP Server From a Legacy One

cite.text: A client that supports both modern (per-request-metadata) MCP versions and a legacy version that requires an `initialize` handshake MAY detect which era the server implements by attempting a modern request first. On `400 Bad Request`, the client SHOULD inspect the response body before falling back: modern servers also use `400` for [`UnsupportedProtocolVersionError`][unsupported-version], `MissingRequiredClientCapabilityError`, and header-validation failures.

q.en: A client's cached assumption that a particular server is modern turns out to be wrong on the next call. What does the spec say the client may do?

o.en: Nothing at all; a cached era decision can never be revisited later on
Re-probe the server, since a cached era may be rechecked later if it fails
Permanently block that whole server address for every other client that connects
Switch every other cached server's era over to legacy as a precaution

x.en: Clients should cache the era decision for the life of the process or origin, and may re-probe if that cached assumption later fails.

questions.setTitle: Telling a Modern MCP Server From a Legacy One

cite.text: The era determination is a property of the server, not of an individual request. Clients SHOULD cache the result for the lifetime of the server process (stdio) or origin (HTTP), and MAY persist it across restarts of the same server configuration, re-probing if the cached assumption later fails.

q.en: What does 2026-07-28 remove that a client written for the current revision should never send to a modern server?

o.en: A tools/call request that names a tool the server has never listed
A server/discover request sent before any other request on the connection
A request opening the connection with a version and capability handshake
A resources/read request naming a URI the server does not recognize

x.en: The handshake and the session it used to open a connection are gone in 2026-07-28; every request now carries its own version and capabilities in _meta.

questions.setTitle: Telling a Modern MCP Server From a Legacy One

cite.text: Make MCP stateless: remove the `initialize`/`notifications/initialized` handshake. Every request now carries its protocol version and client capabilities in `_meta` (`io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion`, `io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities`). Clients SHOULD identify themselves on each request (`io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo`), and servers SHOULD identify themselves in each result's `_meta` (`io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo`). Version mismatches return `UnsupportedProtocolVersionError` (SEP-2575).

q.en: A host application needs data from three different MCP servers in one session. How many MCP client instances does the host create to do this?

o.en: Two clients, since one client can safely serve two servers at once
Three clients, each holding a dedicated connection to one server
One client that opens three separate connections in turn
Zero, because the host process talks to servers directly without a client layer

x.en: The host embeds exactly one client per server connection, so three connected servers require three separate client instances, each bound to exactly one server.

questions.setTitle: Hosts, Clients, and Servers: MCP's Process Topology

cite.text: MCP follows a client-server architecture where an MCP host — an AI application like Claude Code or Claude Desktop — establishes connections to one or more MCP servers.
