The MCP host accomplishes this by creating one MCP client for each MCP server. Each MCP client maintains a dedicated connection with its corresponding MCP server.

q.en: A filesystem server launches as a local subprocess over stdio, while a billing server runs on another company's infrastructure and is reached over Streamable HTTP. What follows from that difference?

o.en: Streamable HTTP servers can only expose resources and prompts, never tools
The stdio server must use OAuth while the HTTP server reads credentials from the environment
The local server crosses a process boundary, the remote one a network boundary
Nothing changes: MCP message shapes stay identical no matter which transport carries them

x.en: Local stdio servers are separate processes on the same machine while remote Streamable HTTP servers cross a network boundary, and a server's trust considerations follow whichever boundary it actually crosses.

questions.setTitle: Hosts, Clients, and Servers: MCP's Process Topology

cite.text: Note that MCP server refers to the program that serves context data, regardless of where it runs. MCP servers can execute locally or remotely. For example, when Claude Desktop launches the filesystem server, the server runs locally on the same machine because it uses the STDIO transport. This is commonly referred to as a "local" MCP server. The official Sentry MCP server runs on the Sentry platform, and uses the Streamable HTTP transport. This is commonly referred to as a "remote" MCP server.

q.en: Which pairing correctly matches an MCP server primitive with who decides when it is used?

o.en: Tools are user-controlled, resources are model-controlled, prompts are application-driven
Resources are model-controlled, prompts are application-driven, tools are user-controlled
All three primitives are selected by the server operator before the connection opens
Tools are model-controlled, resources are application-driven, prompts are user-controlled

x.en: The model decides when to call a tool, the host application decides which resources enter context, and the user explicitly selects which prompt to run.

questions.setTitle: Hosts, Clients, and Servers: MCP's Process Topology

cite.text: Prompts are designed to be user-controlled, meaning they are exposed from servers to clients with the intention of the user being able to explicitly select them for use. This refers to who decides when the prompt is used, not who authors its content. Prompt content is defined by the server.

q.en: A server wants an on-demand language model completion routed through the client's own model access, without embedding a model SDK itself. Which client feature exists for that, and what is its status in 2026-07-28?

o.en: Sampling, which is deprecated with a migration to LLM provider APIs directly
Elicitation, and it is the current, actively recommended mechanism for this
Logging, and it is deprecated with a migration to stderr or OpenTelemetry
Roots, and it is deprecated with a migration to passing paths as tool arguments

x.en: Sampling lets a server ask the client to run a model completion on its behalf, but it is deprecated in 2026-07-28 and new implementations should call LLM provider APIs directly instead.

questions.setTitle: Hosts, Clients, and Servers: MCP's Process Topology

cite.text: Deprecated: The Sampling feature is deprecated as of protocol version `2026-07-28` (SEP-2577). Under the feature lifecycle policy, it remains in the specification for at least twelve months after this revision's release before it becomes eligible for removal. New implementations SHOULD NOT adopt it; existing implementations SHOULD migrate to integrating directly with LLM provider APIs. See the deprecated features registry.

q.en: Two independently written servers both self-report serverInfo.name as "primary" during server/discover, yet a host aggregating both must still route tool calls to the correct one. What does the host key its routing on?

o.en: The protocol version string that server declares in its capabilities
The connection identifier the host itself assigned when it connected
Whichever server happens to answer the discovery request first
The self-reported serverInfo.name value returned by that server's discover result

x.en: serverInfo is self-reported and never guaranteed unique across independently written servers, so a host must route by the connection identifier it assigned itself, not by a server's own claimed name.

questions.setTitle: Hosts, Clients, and Servers: MCP's Process Topology

cite.text: The server `name` (from `serverInfo`) is not guaranteed to be unique across servers and SHOULD NOT be relied upon for disambiguation.

q.en: A host connects to a files server and a notes server. Both declare a tool literally named search. After the host builds its aggregated registry, how does it expose the second one?

o.en: It merges both into a single combined search tool that queries both servers at once
It silently overwrites the first entry so only the newest search remains
It disambiguates the collision, for example by prefixing the second search with a server identifier
It drops the second search tool entirely so the model never sees it

x.en: Tool name uniqueness is scoped to a single server, so collisions across servers are normal. The specification says aggregating clients SHOULD implement a disambiguation strategy such as prefixing tool names with a server identifier, and SHOULD NOT rely on serverInfo.name, which is not guaranteed unique. Merging, overwriting or dropping a tool would hide a real tool from the model.

questions.setTitle: Hosts, Clients, and Servers: MCP's Process Topology

review.note: Opzione C e spiegazione allineate alla spec: la spec chiede una strategia di disambiguazione (per esempio un prefisso con l'identificatore del server), non impone di tenere il primo nome come canonico. / Aligned with the spec: it asks for a disambiguation strategy such as a server-id prefix, it does not mandate keeping the first name canonical.

cite.text: Tool name uniqueness is scoped to a single server. Clients or proxies that aggregate tools from multiple servers MAY encounter naming collisions (for example, two servers each exposing a `search` tool) and SHOULD implement a disambiguation strategy such as prefixing tool names with a server identifier.

q.en: A client wants a server's identity, supported protocol versions, and capabilities in a single round trip before it sends anything else. Which request gives it all three together?

o.en: resources/list, which returns the server's readable resources and their URIs
server/discover, which returns supported versions, capabilities, and identity together
prompts/list, which returns the reusable templates a user can select
the initialize handshake, which a connection completes before any request

x.en: server/discover is the single request built for this: its DiscoverResult carries supportedVersions, capabilities, and the server's self-reported identity together, and the 2026-07-28 revision removed the initialize handshake entirely.

questions.setTitle: Discovering a Server and Negotiating What It Can Do

cite.text: `server/discover` lets a client query a server's supported protocol versions, capabilities, and identity before sending any other requests. Servers MUST implement it.

q.en: Which statement correctly describes when server/discover must be implemented and when it must be called?

o.en: Neither side is required to support it, since it is purely experimental tooling
Clients must call it before any other request, and servers may skip implementing it
Servers must implement it, and clients may call it or skip it entirely
Both sides must implement it and call it exactly once per connection

x.en: The specification requires every server to implement server/discover, but calling it is optional for a client, which may send any request directly and handle a version error if one comes back.

questions.setTitle: Discovering a Server and Negotiating What It Can Do

cite.text: Clients that want to select a version up front can call `server/discover`, a mandatory RPC that returns the server's supported protocol versions, capabilities, and identity in a single request. Calling it is optional: a client is free to send any request directly and handle a version error if one comes back.

q.en: A tools/call request omits the elicitation capability from clientCapabilities, but the tool being called needs it to ask a follow-up question mid call. What does a conformant server do?

o.en: It proceeds anyway and silently skips the follow-up question to stay fast
It returns a tools/call error -32602 because the arguments fail the input schema
It queues the call and waits for the client to reconnect with elicitation enabled
It returns MissingRequiredClientCapabilityError, code -32021, naming exactly which capability the request lacked

x.en: A server must not rely on a capability the client did not declare on that request, so it returns -32021 with data.requiredCapabilities naming exactly what the client needs to declare before retrying.

questions.setTitle: Discovering a Server and Negotiating What It Can Do

cite.text: A server MUST NOT rely on capabilities the client has not declared. If processing a request requires a capability the client did not include in `io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities`, the server MUST return a `MissingRequiredClientCapabilityError` (`-32021`) whose `data.requiredCapabilities` lists the missing capabilities. On HTTP, the response status MUST be `400 Bad Request`.

q.en: A client sends a request naming an older protocol version to a server whose supportedVersions list does not include it. What should the client do next?

o.en: Retry the same request with a version taken from the error data
Treat the server as unreachable and stop sending it any further requests
Fall back to the initialize handshake from the earlier revision
Resend the identical request unchanged, since the server retries automatically

Only the clientCapabilities included in that request's own _meta, checked fresh
Whatever the server advertised in its own DiscoverResult earlier in the exchange
Whatever capabilities the client declared on its very first request to it

Display, logging, and debugging, never a security or authorization decision
Authenticating the server before the client sends its first real request

type object with additionalProperties false, accepting only empty objects

The server's source repository, since none of the wire messages can be trusted at all

Nothing at all, since x-mcp-header only mirrors a value the client already sent in the request body

q.en: A registry server.json declares the name acme-tools with no further structure. Why does this fail a reviewer's check?

As a prompt-injection risk, since instructions is self-reported text aimed at steering the model's behavior

q.en: A client sends prompts/list with a cursor value the server never issued. What should a conformant server do with that request?

It is chosen by the server and returned to the client inside requestState itself

Cache it alongside the tool definition so future calls can reuse the same value

o.en: Only requests that already carry a progressToken value inside their _meta block
tools/call, prompts/get, and resources/read, and nothing else at all in the protocol

The client must poll the tool list again before any change becomes visible
A reply closes the request it answers, leaving nothing open for the change
JSON-RPC does not allow a server to send an unsolicited message at all

x.en: A JSON-RPC reply is tied to the one request it closes, so an ongoing change with no request in flight needs a notification on a stream instead.

q.en: A client opens a subscriptions/listen stream with a fresh request id. What must the very first message on that stream be?

o.en: resources/subscribe, confirming the resource watch was registered successfully
an empty tools/list result that only confirms the new stream opened
notifications/resources/updated, reporting whatever the server produces first
notifications/subscriptions/acknowledged, carrying the listen request id as subscriptionId

x.en: The server must send the acknowledgment first, and it carries the id of that listen request as the subscription id in _meta, before any other notification on that stream.

On stdio, where every subscription shares one channel, this ordering is defined per subscription ID and not per channel: messages belonging to other subscriptions MAY be interleaved before it.

q.en: A tools/call request includes a progressToken and the server reports progress while it runs. Where do those progress notifications appear?

o.en: Only on the same request response channel, never on a listen stream
On a separate logging channel that is gated by a logLevel setting
On whichever stream last acknowledged a subscription for that client
On the subscriptions/listen stream, tagged with that same subscription id

The server's response is itself an SSE stream that stays open and delivers the change notifications the client opted in to (such as `notifications/tools/list_changed` or `notifications/resources/updated`). Request-scoped notifications like `notifications/progress` and `notifications/message` are not delivered on the listen stream — they flow only on the response stream of the request they relate to.

Send a notifications/cancelled notification that names the exact request id
Send a fresh tools/call for the same id with an empty arguments object
Wait, since stdio has no way to cancel a request once it starts

q.en: A server ends a subscription during a planned shutdown, rather than the connection simply dropping. What should it send before closing the stream?

A result for the original listen request, complete, with the subscription id

The result carries no method-specific data beyond the standard result fields and subscription metadata. This is the JSON-RPC response to the long-lived request, correlated by its `id`, and signals that the subscription ended gracefully — as opposed to an abrupt transport drop, which carries no response.

o.en: Respond 401 Unauthorized instead, since Origin is treated as authentication proof.
Log the mismatch but continue processing the request as usual.
Respond 403 Forbidden, since this defends against DNS rebinding attacks.
Accept it anyway if the request also carries a valid bearer token.

x.en: Streamable HTTP servers validate the Origin header on every connection to prevent DNS rebinding attacks and respond 403 Forbidden when it is present and not allowed; Origin validation is a defense in addition to authentication, not a substitute for it.

questions.setTitle: Transports and the HTTP Header Contract

cite.text: Servers MUST validate the `Origin` header on all incoming connections to prevent DNS rebinding attacks. - If the `Origin` header is present and invalid, servers MUST respond with HTTP 403 Forbidden. The HTTP response body MAY comprise a JSON-RPC _error response_ that has no `id`. 2. When running locally, servers SHOULD bind only to localhost (127.0.0.1) rather than all network interfaces (0.0.0.0). 3. Servers SHOULD implement proper authentication for all connections.

q.en: A client sends an HTTP GET to the MCP endpoint, expecting the old standalone event stream to open. How does a modern 2026-07-28 server respond?

o.en: With 404 Not Found, since GET was never part of any MCP transport.
By opening an SSE stream and sending an endpoint event, as before.
By minting a fresh Mcp-Session-Id and starting a new session for it.
With 405 Method Not Allowed, since the modern endpoint only accepts POST.

x.en: The 2026-07-28 Streamable HTTP transport removed the standalone GET stream and protocol sessions; a modern server answers GET or DELETE on the MCP endpoint with 405 Method Not Allowed instead of opening the deprecated HTTP+SSE event stream.

questions.setTitle: Transports and the HTTP Header Contract

cite.text: HTTP GET or DELETE to the MCP endpoint: respond with `405 Method Not Allowed`. - An `Mcp-Session-Id` header on a request: ignore it, and do not mint or echo session IDs. - A `Last-Event-ID` header: ignore it; streams are not resumable.

q.en: Why does an accepted notification POST return 202 Accepted with no body, instead of a JSON-RPC result?

o.en: Because a notification never gets a JSON-RPC reply; only its delivery is acknowledged.
Because notifications always fail validation, so the server returns nothing useful.
Because 202 itself carries a JSON-RPC result whose resultType is accepted.
Because the client already learns the outcome from the Mcp-Method header alone.

x.en: A notification has no id and never receives a JSON-RPC response; the transport instead acknowledges its delivery with HTTP 202 Accepted and no body, which is a transport-level outcome rather than a JSON-RPC result carrying a resultType.

questions.setTitle: Transports and the HTTP Header Contract

cite.text: If the server accepts it, the server MUST return HTTP status code `202 Accepted` with no body.

q.en: Which two fields does a complete resources/read or resources/list result always carry?

o.en: A cursor value and an echoed requestState from the prior call
A Mcp-Session-Id header value and a Last-Event-ID stream marker
A protocolVersion string and a clientCapabilities object under _meta
An integer ttlMs and a cacheScope of public or private

x.en: A complete result from any of the six cacheable operations must carry an integer ttlMs of zero or more and a cacheScope of public or private, the fields SEP-2549 added for the 2026-07-28 caching rules.

cite.text: Cacheable Results in MCP use two fields to provide caching hints to clients:

q.en: A resources/read result for a caller's private note comes back with cacheScope set to private. What does that field actually control?

o.en: It limits reuse of the cached bytes to the same authorization context as before
It tells the client to encrypt the cached bytes before writing them to disk
It grants any caller who reuses the cache full read access to that note
It replaces the need for the server to check the caller's access on future calls

x.en: cacheScope only tells a cache who may store and replay the bytes; it is never a substitute for the server's own per-primitive access control on each request.

cite.text: `"private"` | The response contains private data that is not meant to be shared between callers. Cached responses MAY be reused for the same authorization context. Caches MUST NOT be shared across authorization contexts (e.g. a different access token requires a different cache).

q.en: A resources/list response carries nextCursor set to an empty string. What should a conformant client do next?

o.en: Report -32602 because an empty cursor value is never valid on the wire
Send the same empty cursor value back, since it is a valid list position
Treat the empty string as the end of the list and stop paginating
Restart pagination from the very beginning by omitting the cursor field entirely

x.en: An empty string is a legal opaque cursor; only the absence of nextCursor signals the end of a list, so a client that treats an empty string as the end will stop paginating one page too early.

cite.text: Don't make any determination based on cursor value other than whether a non-null value was provided (e.g. an empty string is a valid cursor and thus MUST NOT be treated as the end of results)

q.en: A client retries a resources/read request after answering an input_required elicitation. Under the 2026-07-28 caching rules, what happens to the completed result that comes back?

o.en: It is cached only if the server also set listChanged to true in its capabilities
It is cached with a cacheScope of public regardless of the resource's real scope
It is never cached, because it depended on inputResponses outside the cache key
It is cached under the original request's id so the retry never has to repeat

x.en: Results produced by retrying an MRTR request carry inputResponses that are not part of the cache key, so the specification requires clients to skip caching them even though the result itself still reports ttlMs and cacheScope.

cite.text: Results produced by retrying a request through the multi round-trip requests mechanism—that is, requests carrying `inputResponses` or `requestState`—MUST NOT be cached, as they depend on inputs that are not part of the cache key.

q.en: A client's cached tools/list entry still has two minutes left on its ttlMs when a notifications/tools/list_changed notification arrives on the listen stream. What should the client do?

o.en: Extend the TTL window, since a notification proves the server is still reachable
Wait for the TTL to expire naturally before treating the entry as stale
Ignore the notification, since the cached entry is still inside its TTL window
Treat the entry as stale right away and refetch it when next needed

x.en: TTL and push notifications are complementary: a relevant list_changed notification invalidates a cached response immediately, overriding however much time was left on the TTL clock.

cite.text: When a relevant notification is received while a cached response is still fresh, the notification invalidates the cached response and it should be considered immediately stale.

q.en: Besides helping a client's own cache and pagination stay predictable, why does the specification recommend that tools/list return entries in a deterministic order?

o.en: A stable prefix lets an upstream provider's own prompt cache hit more often
A stable order lets a client skip sending clientCapabilities on repeated tools/list calls
A stable order is required before a server may advertise the listChanged capability at all
A stable order is the only way a cursor can ever be treated as opaque

x.en: When a tool catalog serializes identically every time, an LLM provider's own prompt caching can reuse the cached prefix instead of reprocessing it, a real latency and cost benefit distinct from MCP's own ttlMs mechanism.

cite.text: Servers SHOULD return tools in a deterministic order (i.e., the same ordering across requests when the underlying set of tools has not changed). Deterministic ordering enables clients to reliably cache the tool list and improves LLM prompt cache hit rates when tools are included in model context.

q.en: Why can a server not just hold the connection open until a twenty-minute pipeline finishes?

o.en: Transport timeouts, no input channel during execution, and no crash recovery at all
Because MCP requires every tool call to use the tasks extension for any tool
Because the client always closes the connection after exactly one request completes
Because JSON-RPC forbids any request from taking longer than one second to answer

x.en: Blocking runs into transport timeouts that are not the server's to set, no channel to ask for input mid-call, and no way to recover after a crash or dropped connection.

questions.setTitle: Long-Running Work and the Tasks Extension

cite.text: You could hold the connection open until the work finishes. Tasks solve problems that blocking cannot:

q.en: Where does a client declare support for io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks on a given request?

o.en: In the tasks field of the tools/list response the server returned earlier
In that request's own params._meta, under clientCapabilities.extensions field
In a session header the server issues after the first successful tool call
In a one-time initialize handshake that both sides remember for the connection

x.en: Extension support is declared per request in clientCapabilities.extensions inside params._meta, because there is no session or handshake that would let the server remember an earlier declaration.

questions.setTitle: Long-Running Work and the Tasks Extension

cite.text: The Tasks extension is specified in the ext-tasks repository. It uses the standard MCP extension negotiation mechanism: clients declare support in the `extensions` field of the `io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities` they send in each request's `_meta`, and servers advertise theirs in the capabilities returned by `server/discover`.

q.en: A tasks/get response shows resultType complete and, nested inside it, status working. What does that combination mean?

o.en: Both the poll request and the underlying job have now fully finished
The client must resend tools/call to keep the underlying job moving forward
The poll request itself succeeded, but the underlying job is still running
The server rejected the poll because the task is not ready to be read

x.en: tasks/get always completes, so its own resultType is complete; the job's real state travels in the separate, nested status field, which here still says working.

questions.setTitle: Long-Running Work and the Tasks Extension

cite.text: The response carries the appropriate response variant for the task's current status (see Task Status). The `resultType` field MUST be set to `"complete"` on this object as it is the standard result shape for the `tasks/get` request.

q.en: A task moves to input_required and tasks/get returns an inputRequests map. How does the client respond?

o.en: It waits, since input_required tasks resume automatically without any reply at all
It retries the original tools/call with a new id and the same inputRequests key
It sends a fresh elicitation/create request directly to the server on its own
It sends tasks/update with inputResponses keyed to the still outstanding entries

x.en: Task input is answered through tasks/update with inputResponses keyed to the outstanding entries; the client never resends the original tools/call for this.

questions.setTitle: Long-Running Work and the Tasks Extension

cite.text: `input_required`: The server needs input from the client before the task can proceed. The `tasks/get` response will include outstanding requests in the `inputRequests` field. The client MUST inspect this field and SHOULD provide responses via the `inputResponses` field in subsequent `tasks/update` requests.

q.en: A tools/call finishes with isError true inside its content. What status does its task reach?

o.en: completed, because the tool call still produced its own normally defined result
cancelled, because an error inside a result counts as an implicit cancellation
input_required, because the model must approve the error before it counts at all
failed, because any error anywhere in the result is treated as a JSON-RPC failure

x.en: A tool result with isError true is still a successful protocol exchange, so the task reaches completed; failed is reserved for a JSON-RPC error during execution, not a tool-level failure.

questions.setTitle: Long-Running Work and the Tasks Extension

cite.text: For tool calls that complete successfully at the protocol level but return an tool-level error (indicated by `isError: true` in the tool result), the task reaches `completed` status with the tool result in the `result` field:

q.en: Which piece of work is the best fit for the tasks extension rather than a plain call or an MRTR round trip?

o.en: Reading one resource whose contents never change between separate requests
A deploy pipeline that may pause for approval and could outlive a timeout
Listing the tools a server currently exposes to a newly connecting client
Asking the user to confirm a single value before finishing the current request

x.en: A task earns its added complexity when work might outlive a timeout, pause for input mid-execution, or need to survive a restart or cancellation, unlike the other options here.

questions.setTitle: Long-Running Work and the Tasks Extension

cite.text: Not every tool call returns instantly. Some operations — CI pipelines, batch processing, human approvals — take seconds, minutes, or longer. MCP Tasks let servers return a durable handle instead of blocking, so clients can poll for progress, provide input when needed, and retrieve the final result after reconnecting.

q.en: In an MCP exchange, which two participants sit inside the same trust domain that the host directly controls?

o.en: The host and the client it runs
The client and every server it has connected to
The server and the tools it exposes
The model and the upstream systems a server calls

x.en: The host owns the client it runs and both sit inside one trust domain, while the server is a separate program the host does not control.

questions.setTitle: Trust Zones in an MCP Exchange

q.en: A server's discover result carries a flattering serverInfo.name. What should a host's trust decision rely on instead?

o.en: The title field inside the server's tool annotations
The identity the host recorded when it connected the server
The name the server reports in its serverInfo field
The name shown in the server's most recent tool description

x.en: clientInfo and serverInfo are self-reported and unverified, so a host must base trust decisions on its own record of which server it connected, never on what the connection claims about itself.

questions.setTitle: Trust Zones in an MCP Exchange

cite.text: `serverInfo` is self-reported by the server and is not verified by the protocol. It is intended for display, logging, and debugging. Clients SHOULD NOT use it to change their behavior, and SHOULD NOT rely on it for security decisions.

q.en: A tool from a server that is not on the host's trusted list declares destructiveHint as false. How should the host treat that claim when making a safety decision?

o.en: Accept it only when the tool's description also sounds harmless
Accept it, since annotations describe exactly what a tool does
Ignore the claim and fall back to the destructive default
Reject the tool outright and remove it from the tool list

x.en: Tool annotations are hints that clients must treat as untrusted unless the server is trusted, so an untrusted claim of destructiveHint false falls back to the conservative default of true.

questions.setTitle: Trust Zones in an MCP Exchange

cite.text: For trust & safety and security, clients MUST consider tool annotations to be untrusted unless they come from trusted servers.

q.en: A tool definition includes an icon whose src is javascript:alert(1). What must a conformant client do with that icon?

o.en: Render the icon inside a sandboxed iframe with scripts disabled
Convert the icon to a data URI before rendering it safely
Render the icon only after asking the user for permission
Reject the icon, since its scheme is not https or data

x.en: Clients must reject icon URIs that use unsafe schemes such as javascript, file, or ftp, accepting only https and data URIs for icon sources.

questions.setTitle: Trust Zones in an MCP Exchange

cite.text: Ensure that the icon URI is either a HTTPS or `data:` URI. Clients MUST reject icon URIs that use unsafe schemes and redirects, such as `javascript:`, `file:`, `ftp:`, `ws:`, or local app URI schemes.

q.en: A tool result from a notes server contains text instructing the host to call a delete tool on a separate ticket server. What should the host do?

o.en: Refuse the call, since crossing servers is the model's choice
Ask the notes server to confirm the instruction before proceeding
Execute the call, since the notes server is already connected
Forward the instruction to the ticket server as a routine notification

x.en: Content one server returns is untrusted data, so an instruction embedded inside it must never trigger a call to a different server. Only a choice the model makes on its own may cross that boundary.

questions.setTitle: Trust Zones in an MCP Exchange

q.en: Which practice matches MCP's guidance for a locally launched stdio server that needs credentials?

o.en: Request the credentials through a server-initiated sampling request
Read credentials from the environment instead of running an OAuth flow
Run the full OAuth 2.1 authorization code flow over the stdio transport
Embed a long-lived token inside the server's published package

x.en: stdio implementations should not run the OAuth flow and instead read credentials from the environment, since the transport already runs inside the user's own trust domain.

questions.setTitle: Trust Zones in an MCP Exchange

cite.text: The OAuth flow in this guide is for HTTP-based transports. Servers that use the stdio transport should retrieve credentials from the environment instead. They run locally, so they can also use credentials from libraries embedded in the server.

q.en: Before a client has ever authenticated to a particular MCP server, what is the very first sign that the server requires authorization?

o.en: The server's tools/list result silently omits every tool until login completes
A tools/call receives a plain HTTP 401 response with no JSON-RPC body
The server requires a legacy initialize handshake to complete before any token is issued
The client's connection attempt times out repeatedly until credentials are supplied

x.en: An unauthenticated request is rejected at the HTTP layer with a 401 before it is ever parsed as a protocol message, so there is no result or error body to read.

questions.setTitle: Authorizing Access to an MCP Server

cite.text: MCP clients MUST be able to parse `WWW-Authenticate` headers and respond appropriately to `HTTP 401 Unauthorized` responses from the MCP server.

q.en: A 401 response's WWW-Authenticate header does not include a resource_metadata value. What must the client do next to find the Protected Resource Metadata document?

o.en: Ask the user to paste the authorization server's URL into a configuration file
Abort the flow immediately, since the header is the only discovery path the specification allows
Fall back to the well-known URIs, trying the path-specific location before the root
Fall back to the well-known URIs, trying the root location before the path-specific one

x.en: When the header omits resource_metadata, the client must construct the well-known URIs itself and try the path-specific location before falling back to the root.

questions.setTitle: Authorizing Access to an MCP Server

cite.text: MCP clients MUST support both discovery mechanisms and use the resource metadata URL from the parsed `WWW-Authenticate` headers when present; otherwise, they MUST fall back to constructing and requesting the well-known URIs in the order listed above.

q.en: An authorization server's issuer is https://auth.example.com/tenant1, a URL with a path component. In which order must a client try metadata endpoints?

o.en: oauth-authorization-server at the root only, since path components are stripped before discovery begins
openid-configuration with the path appended, then oauth-authorization-server with the path inserted, then openid-configuration with the path inserted
openid-configuration with the path inserted only, since MCP does not define an OAuth-specific well-known suffix
oauth-authorization-server with the path inserted, then openid-configuration with the path inserted, then openid-configuration with the path appended

x.en: For a path issuer the client tries OAuth metadata with the path inserted, then OpenID Connect discovery with the path inserted, then OpenID Connect discovery with the path appended.

questions.setTitle: Authorizing Access to an MCP Server

cite.text: OAuth 2.0 Authorization Server Metadata with path insertion: `https://auth.example.com/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server/tenant1` 2. OpenID Connect Discovery 1.0 with path insertion: `https://auth.example.com/.well-known/openid-configuration/tenant1` 3. OpenID Connect Discovery 1.0 path appending: `https://auth.example.com/tenant1/.well-known/openid-configuration`

q.en: MCP servers MUST validate an incoming bearer token's audience before accepting a call. What does that check actually verify?

o.en: That the token was issued specifically for this MCP server's own canonical URI
That the token carries every scope the requested tool could ever need
That the token has not expired since the authorization server issued it
That the token was issued by an authorization server the client has used before

x.en: Audience validation confirms the token names this server's own canonical resource URI, which is why a well-formed token issued for a different server must still be rejected.

questions.setTitle: Authorizing Access to an MCP Server

cite.text: MCP servers MUST validate access tokens before processing the request, ensuring the access token is issued specifically for the MCP server, and take all necessary steps to ensure no data is returned to unauthorized parties.

q.en: A client is about to redirect a user's browser to an authorization server for the first time in this flow. What must it do before sending that redirect, to defend against a mix-up attack?

o.en: Request a fresh access token first, then discard it once the redirect completes
Record the expected issuer from the validated metadata to compare against the returned iss value
Cache the authorization server's TLS certificate fingerprint and compare it once the redirect returns
Register a brand-new redirect URI just for this one authorization attempt

x.en: RFC 9207 mix-up defenses depend on the client recording the expected issuer before redirecting and comparing it exactly against the iss value the authorization response returns.

questions.setTitle: Authorizing Access to an MCP Server

cite.text: Before redirecting the user-agent, the client MUST record the `issuer` value from the selected authorization server's validated metadata document (see Authorization Server Metadata Discovery) and associate it with the same per-request record used to store the PKCE code verifier (and the `state` value, if used). The validation in this section depends on that recorded value being authentic; it provides no protection if the expected issuer was obtained from an unvalidated source.

q.en: A resource server receives a token that is well formed and unexpired, but was issued with an audience naming a different MCP server. What should it do?

o.en: Accept the call, since a well-formed token from a known authorization server can be trusted
Forward the token to the intended server and proxy the response back to the caller
Reject the call with 401 Unauthorized, since the token is not valid for this server
Reject the call with 403 Forbidden, since the token lacks a required scope

x.en: A token whose audience names a different server is invalid for this one regardless of its signature or expiry, so the server rejects it with 401, not a scope-related 403.

questions.setTitle: Authorizing Access to an MCP Server

cite.text: Audience. Your MCP server must reject tokens that weren't issued for it. The `resource` value from the client should become the token's audience, which is the `aud` claim in a JWT. Some products need a setting for this, or let you configure the audience on a scope instead. Others always use their own identifier. In that case, compare the audience with that identifier, and keep your server's URL as the PRM `resource`. The identifier must belong to this MCP server only, so don't share one application registration between servers.

q.en: An MCP client is about to connect to a server whose authorization server it has never used before, and the client already has information on file for that authorization server. Per the specification's registration priority order, what should the client do?

o.en: Register a brand new client through Dynamic Client Registration to avoid using stale credentials
Use the pre-registered credentials it already has on file for that authorization server
Prompt the person to type in a client id before any request is sent to the server
Fetch a Client ID Metadata Document anyway, since that path is always preferred over stored information

x.en: Pre-registered credentials come first in the priority order; a client only turns to Client ID Metadata Documents, then Dynamic Client Registration, then the user, when nothing is already on file for that issuer.

questions.setTitle: Proving a Client's Identity to an Authorization Server

cite.text: Clients that use pre-registered credentials, or persist client credentials obtained via Dynamic Client Registration, MUST associate those credentials with the specific authorization server that issued them, keyed by the authorization server's `issuer` identifier. When the authorization server changes (detected via updated protected resource metadata), clients MUST NOT reuse client credentials from a different authorization server and MUST re-register with the new authorization server.

q.en: A Client ID Metadata Document is fetched from https://app.example.com/oauth/client.json. Which property must the authorization server confirm before it trusts the document?

o.en: The document was fetched over plain HTTP so the authorization server can cache it
The document was registered ahead of time through a registration_endpoint call
The document's client_id field matches that URL exactly, character for character
The document includes a client secret the authorization server can verify locally

x.en: The authorization server must validate that the client_id inside the fetched document equals the URL it was fetched from exactly; a mismatch means the document cannot be trusted as that client's identity.

questions.setTitle: Proving a Client's Identity to an Authorization Server

cite.text: MUST validate that the fetched document's `client_id` matches the URL exactly

q.en: A desktop CLI tool registers through Dynamic Client Registration and redirects to http://127.0.0.1:PORT/callback. Which application_type should it declare?

o.en: confidential, because a CLI tool can store a client secret safely on local disk
It should omit application_type, since non-OIDC servers always ignore that field
web, because the authorization server only reads application_type for browser clients
native, because the tool is a locally hosted application reached through localhost

x.en: Native applications, including desktop tools, CLIs, and locally hosted apps reached through localhost, should declare application_type native; omitting it defaults to web under OIDC and can conflict with a localhost redirect URI.

questions.setTitle: Proving a Client's Identity to an Authorization Server

cite.text: Native applications (desktop applications, mobile apps, CLI tools, and locally-hosted web applications accessed via `localhost`) SHOULD use `application_type: "native"` - Web applications (remote browser-based applications served from a non-local host) SHOULD use `application_type: "web"`

q.en: A client's persisted credentials were issued by authorization server A. The protected resource metadata for the same MCP server now names authorization server B instead. What must the client do?

o.en: Treat the credentials as invalid for B, and register again with the correct server
Merge both authorization servers into one trust domain sharing a single client id
Forward the credentials from A to B and let B decide whether to accept them
Keep using the credentials from A, since the resource server itself has not changed

x.en: Credentials are bound to the issuer that issued them; when the authorization server changes, the client must not reuse the old credentials and must re-register with the new one.

questions.setTitle: Proving a Client's Identity to an Authorization Server

cite.text: Clients that use pre-registered credentials, or persist client credentials obtained via Dynamic Client Registration, MUST associate those credentials with the specific authorization server that issued them, keyed by the authorization server's `issuer` identifier. When the authorization server changes (detected via updated protected resource metadata), clients MUST NOT reuse client credentials from a different authorization server and MUST re-register with the new authorization server.

q.en: An MCP proxy uses one static client id to reach a third-party authorization server on behalf of many dynamically registered downstream clients. What does the specification require of that proxy?

o.en: Nothing extra, because the static client id already represents every downstream client
It must obtain the user's consent for each dynamically registered client before forwarding
It must disable Dynamic Client Registration entirely for every downstream client it serves
It must rotate the static client id every single time a new downstream client appears

x.en: A proxy using a static client id is a confused deputy risk; the specification requires it to obtain user consent for each dynamically registered client before forwarding that client's request to the third-party authorization server.

questions.setTitle: Proving a Client's Identity to an Authorization Server

cite.text: MCP proxy servers using static client IDs MUST obtain user consent for each dynamically registered client before forwarding to third-party authorization servers (which may require additional consent).

q.en: A CI pipeline needs to call an MCP server on a nightly schedule with no person available to approve access. Which mechanism fits, and how must the server learn the client supports it?

o.en: Dynamic Client Registration, because it is the only flow built for an unattended client
Enterprise-Managed Authorization, since it removes the need for any access token entirely
The OAuth Client Credentials extension, declared in the client's per-request capabilities
The standard interactive authorization code flow, approved once in advance by an administrator

x.en: Machine-to-machine access without an interactive user fits the OAuth Client Credentials extension, which a client declares in io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities.extensions on each request; extensions are opt-in and never active by default.

questions.setTitle: Proving a Client's Identity to an Authorization Server

cite.text: The OAuth Client Credentials extension solves this by letting a client authenticate using application-level credentials (a client ID and secret, or a signed JWT assertion) rather than delegated user credentials. The client proves its identity directly to the authorization server, which issues an access token without requiring a browser redirect or user interaction.

q.en: A destructive tool call needs a human to approve it before the server will run it. How does the server ask for that approval in MCP 2026-07-28?

o.en: It sends a fresh server-initiated request straight to the client over the still-open connection right away without delay
It returns an input_required result carrying an elicitation/create request, and the client retries with an answer
It refuses the call with a JSON-RPC error until a person runs a separate approval step
It opens a brand new Mcp-Session-Id scoped to this approval and simply waits on that session

x.en: Servers never push requests to the client; a tools/call that needs human approval returns resultType input_required with an elicitation/create inputRequest, and the client answers by retrying with inputResponses and a new id.

cite.text: *Server-to-client interactions (MRTR). When the server needs input from the client — sampling, elicitation, or roots — it does not send its own JSON-RPC request. It returns an [`InputRequiredResult`][input-required-result] containing `inputRequests`, and the client retries the original request with the matching `inputResponses` (see [Multi Round-Trip Requests][mrtr]):

q.en: A client is requesting an access token for an MCP server for the first time, and the 401 challenge carried no scope parameter at all. Which scopes should the client request?

o.en: A single administrative scope that some human operator chooses on the client's behalf, entirely by hand
No scopes at all, letting the server assign a default working set once the user logs in
Only the scopes the WWW-Authenticate challenge named, or all of scopes_supported if the challenge left that field out
Every scope the authorization server has ever issued to any client, just to save a round trip

x.en: The scope selection strategy is to use the scope from the WWW-Authenticate challenge when one is present, and to fall back to scopes_supported as the minimal starting set when the challenge omits it.

cite.text: The client should request the scopes named in the challenge. If the challenge names none, it should request everything in the PRM document's `scopes_supported`. If that is missing too, it leaves out the `scope` parameter. See Scope Selection Strategy.

q.en: A client already holds a token scoped to files:read. A tool call now gets HTTP 403 with error insufficient_scope and scope files:write. What should the client request next?

o.en: Only files:write, discarding files:read, since the server only asked for the new scope this time only
Every scope the server has ever defined, so no future call can ever trigger a 403 again
Whatever scope the previous tool call in this same session happened to already be using instead
The union of files:read and files:write, so the earlier grant is not lost during re-authorization

x.en: Step-up authorization computes the union of the previously granted scopes and the scopes in the current challenge, so a per-operation scope challenge never silently drops permissions the client already had.

cite.text: Scope accumulation across operations is a client-side responsibility. Clients SHOULD compute the union of previously requested scopes and newly challenged scopes when initiating re-authorization, as described in Step-Up Authorization Flow. This allows servers to remain stateless with respect to client scope sets while ensuring clients do not lose previously granted permissions.

q.en: A user approves the delete_file tool on a server. What does that one approval cover?

o.en: Only delete_file itself; a different tool on that same server still needs its own separate approval
Whatever the destructiveHint annotation on the tool currently claims is safe, even once that value changes
Every tool on that server, because the user already trusts the server as a whole from then on
Every future call to delete_file plus any other tool whose name also happens to start with delete

x.en: Consent is scoped to the exact named tool it was granted for, never to a server, a naming pattern, or a category, so a second sensitive tool always needs its own explicit approval.

q.en: A server's tools/call result comes back with resultType input_required. How must the client's next attempt at that same call be shaped?

o.en: It must reuse the original request id so the server can match the two attempts to each other, always
It must use a new request id, include inputResponses, and echo requestState back byte for byte as received
It must wait for the server to push a follow-up request instead of retrying on its own
It must open a brand new connection to the server so the retry starts from a clean session

x.en: A multi round-trip retry always carries a new JSON-RPC id, gathers answers into inputResponses under the same keys the server used, and echoes requestState byte for byte if the server sent one.

cite.text: After the user fills in the form, the client retries the call with a new `id`. The retry carries the user's answers in `inputResponses`, under the same `bookingConfirmation` key as the server's request, and the exact `requestState` value from the result:

q.en: A caller's token carries only payments:read. The server also exposes a send_payment tool gated on payments:write. What should tools/list return to this caller?

o.en: An error result, because a client should never call tools/list without holding every scope the server defines
The full tool list, but with send_payment marked isError so the model learns not to call it
A tool list that omits send_payment, since the result may vary by the authorization on the request
The full tool list including send_payment, since tools/list must never vary between different callers

x.en: Least privilege applies to list results too: tools/list must not change as a side effect of unrelated requests, but it may vary by the authorization presented, so a caller only sees the tools its current scopes actually permit.

cite.text: Servers that declare the `tools` capability MUST respond to `tools/list` requests with the set of tools currently available to the requesting client. This set MAY be empty and MAY change over time (see List Changed Notification), but MUST NOT vary per-connection or as a side effect of other requests on the connection. The set MAY vary by the authorization presented on the request — for example, returning only the tools the caller's granted scopes permit — since credentials are per-request input, not connection state.

q.en: A gateway asks a human to confirm every destructive tool call, and treats that as its complete security design. Which risk survives this design unchanged?

o.en: A tool call that exceeds its declared timeout and returns after the connection closes
A response that arrives in more than one content block instead of exactly one
A confirmation dialog that renders too slowly for the user to read its contents
A tool description that already embeds an instruction the model follows before any confirmation

x.en: Confirmation only gates the destructive call itself; a poisoned description can already have steered which call the model chose to make or how it filled in the arguments, so descriptions and results have to be treated as untrusted earlier than the confirmation step.

questions.setTitle: Risk and Safety Controls for MCP Tool Calls

q.en: A previously approved tool keeps its name and its hash-pinned description, but a fresh discovery response shows a different inputSchema for the same tool. What should a gateway that pins whole descriptors do?

o.en: Quarantine the tool as a rug pull and hold it for re-review before allowing calls again
Accept the change automatically, since the tool's name and description both stayed the same
Ignore the schema field entirely, since only description text can carry an injected instruction
Trust the new schema because its annotations already marked the tool as read only

x.en: Hashing only the description text misses a schema or annotation change, so a whole-descriptor pin catches this drift, and the correct response is to quarantine the tool as a rug pull until someone re-approves the new descriptor and its hash.

questions.setTitle: Risk and Safety Controls for MCP Tool Calls

q.en: A tool handler needs to call an unrelated upstream billing API for the current request, and it has the bearer token the client used to authenticate to the MCP server itself. What must the handler do?

o.en: Forward that same bearer token to the upstream API, since it already proves the user authenticated
Use a separately minted, upstream-scoped credential instead of forwarding the inbound MCP token
Cache the inbound token and reuse it for every future upstream call in the session
Strip the signature from the token and forward only the remaining claims upstream

x.en: Token passthrough, forwarding a token scoped to the MCP server on to an unrelated upstream API, is explicitly forbidden; a compliant handler validates the inbound token for its own purposes and uses a distinct, upstream-scoped credential for the outbound call.

questions.setTitle: Risk and Safety Controls for MCP Tool Calls

cite.text: If the MCP server makes requests to upstream APIs, it may act as an OAuth client to them. The access token used at the upstream API is a separate token, issued by the upstream authorization server. The MCP server MUST NOT pass through the token it received from the MCP client.

q.en: A tool's inputSchema contains a property whose $ref points at https://partner.example/schema.json. Under 2026-07-28, what is the correct handling?

o.en: Replace the $ref with an empty schema object so validation always passes silently
Fetch and cache the schema once, then trust it for every validation after that
Never auto-dereference a network reference by default; treat it as an opt-in, allowlisted fetch
Resolve the reference automatically, since JSON Schema 2020-12 requires every $ref to resolve

x.en: A validator must never auto-dereference a network $ref by default; fetching one, if it is ever necessary, has to be an explicit opt-in behind a host allowlist, a block on private addresses, and a timeout, which is the SSRF defense this lesson's registration check enforces.

questions.setTitle: Risk and Safety Controls for MCP Tool Calls

cite.text: Implementations MAY offer an opt-in mode that fetches non-local `$ref`s but it MUST be disabled by default and SHOULD enforce an allowlist of hosts or at minimum reject loopback, link-local, and private network addresses, apply timeouts and size limits, and log dereferenced URIs.

q.en: A server wants to refuse a tool call because a per-tool rate limit tripped, in a way the model can read and react to. Which response is correct for 2026-07-28?

o.en: A JSON-RPC error using code -32042, reserved for elicitation in the prior revision
A normal result with an empty content list and no isError field at all
A JSON-RPC error using code -32001, a custom code in the legacy range
A normal result with isError set to true and an explanation in its content

x.en: A policy refusal the model should see and possibly adjust for, such as a tripped rate limit or a tool held after a rug pull, belongs in an isError tool execution result; -32001 sits in the legacy -32000 to -32019 block new implementations must not use, and -32042 was retired with the prior revision's elicitation design.

questions.setTitle: Risk and Safety Controls for MCP Tool Calls

cite.text: Tool Execution Errors contain actionable feedback that language models can use to self-correct and retry with adjusted parameters: API failures; Input validation errors (e.g., date in wrong format, value out of range); Business logic errors. They are reported in tool results with isError: true.

q.en: Two independently written MCP servers behind the same gateway both expose a tool literally named search, and neither server knows the other exists. What should the gateway do before exposing either tool to the model?

o.en: Prefix each tool with a stable server identifier so the two names never collide
Drop both tools silently until one of the two servers renames its own tool
Merge both tools into a single entry and pick arguments from whichever call succeeds
Expose whichever server's search tool happened to answer the most recent discover call

x.en: Server names are not guaranteed unique, so an aggregator that lets two identically named tools reach the model risks tool shadowing, where routing silently picks one server's tool for a call meant for the other; the standard fix is a stable, server-qualified prefix on every aggregated name.

questions.setTitle: Risk and Safety Controls for MCP Tool Calls

cite.text: Tool name uniqueness is scoped to a single server. Clients or proxies that aggregate tools from multiple servers MAY encounter naming collisions (for example, two servers each exposing a `search` tool) and SHOULD implement a disambiguation strategy such as prefixing tool names with a server identifier.

q.en: Under the 2026-07-28 stateless model, why can't a server correlate a tool call with an earlier one just from the connection it arrived on?

o.en: A server is required to discard the name of whichever tool a client most recently asked it to run
JSON-RPC forbids a client from ever sending a second request over a connection that is already open
Every request always opens a brand new network connection, so no two requests ever share a transport path at all
A connection carries no assumed meaning between requests, so correlation has to travel explicitly in each request's own metadata

x.en: Because the protocol is stateless, a server must not infer anything from a shared connection, so any correlation identifier, such as a trace id, has to be carried explicitly in the request's own _meta.

questions.setTitle: One Trace ID Ties Auditability to Observability

cite.text: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a stateless protocol: all the information needed to process a request is contained in the request itself. A server processes each request independently; no state should be inferred from previous requests, even those on the same connection or stream.

q.en: A request's _meta carries traceparent: "00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01". What do the third and fourth hyphen-separated segments represent?

o.en: The parent id naming this one span, followed by flags such as whether the trace is sampled
A session identifier the server can use to recall facts learned from that client's earlier requests
A cache key the server hashes together with the method name to look up a stored result
A signature the client generates so the server can verify the request has not been tampered with

x.en: The W3C traceparent format is version-traceid-parentid-flags, so the third segment is the 16-character parent id for this span and the fourth is the flags byte, such as the sampled bit.

questions.setTitle: One Trace ID Ties Auditability to Observability

cite.text: As an exception to the prefix requirement above, the keys `traceparent`, `tracestate`, and `baggage` are reserved for OpenTelemetry trace context propagation. When present, their values MUST follow W3C Trace Context and W3C Baggage formats respectively.

q.en: ops-desk must call credential-vault to finish handling reset_api_key. What should the traceparent on that outbound call contain?

o.en: The exact same traceparent value ops-desk itself received, forwarded to credential-vault without any change at all
The same trace id ops-desk received, paired with a freshly generated parent id for this new hop
No traceparent at all, since credential-vault is a different server and cannot share ops-desk's active trace
A brand new trace id, so credential-vault's own log never mixes with any other server's records

x.en: A well-behaved hop keeps the trace id constant so the whole operation stays correlated, but mints its own fresh parent id rather than reusing the one it received.

questions.setTitle: One Trace ID Ties Auditability to Observability

cite.text: As an exception to the prefix requirement above, the keys `traceparent`, `tracestate`, and `baggage` are reserved for OpenTelemetry trace context propagation. When present, their values MUST follow W3C Trace Context and W3C Baggage formats respectively.

q.en: An audit entry has to record who actually made a tool call. Which value belongs in that field?

o.en: The name field inside the request's self-reported clientInfo block, since it is already sitting in _meta
The server's own serverInfo name, since the server is the one writing the audit entry itself
The principal a validated credential, such as a bearer token, actually resolves to for that request
Whatever free-text label the tool's description happens to suggest for the caller who invoked it

x.en: clientInfo and serverInfo are self-reported and never a security signal, so the audit record's who has to be the authenticated principal a validated credential actually resolves to.

questions.setTitle: One Trace ID Ties Auditability to Observability

q.en: In ops-desk's log, an attacker edits entry 0's arguments and also recomputes entry 0's own stored hash so it matches the new content. What happens when verify() runs next?

o.en: Verification stops running entirely, since patching one entry's hash disables every check after that point
Verification fails immediately at entry 0, regardless of which entry the attacker actually finished editing
Verification passes cleanly, because a hash chain can only ever detect damage to its very last entry
Verification still fails, at entry 1, because its stored prev_hash no longer matches entry 0's new hash

x.en: Patching entry 0's own hash hides the change at entry 0, but entry 1 still stores the original hash as its prev_hash, and that link no longer matches, so the break surfaces one entry later.

questions.setTitle: One Trace ID Ties Auditability to Observability

q.en: ops-desk and credential-vault each keep their own independent hash-chained log. How does a reviewer confirm two entries, one in each, came from the same end-user operation?

o.en: Both entries carry the identical trace id, even though their request ids and their hash chains differ
Both entries carry the identical request id, since every hop of one operation reuses that same id
credential-vault's log silently copies every entry ops-desk already wrote into its own hash chain first
The reviewer matches the two entries' timestamps, since both servers share one synchronized system clock

x.en: Each hop mints its own request id and keeps its own chain, so correlation across servers works only through the one value that stays constant for the whole operation, the trace id.

questions.setTitle: One Trace ID Ties Auditability to Observability

q.en: A team adopts a second AI host for the same internal MCP server. Which statement is true about the server's code?

o.en: It must be rebuilt once for every extra host that joins
It is re-registered by the registry for each new host
It needs a new branch of logic for each host it serves
It answers every host's client with the same result each time

x.en: A server's capability contract is fixed by the specification and does not vary by host, so adding a host is a client-side cost, never a server change.

q.en: On a remote Streamable HTTP deployment with no gateway in front of it, which role implements OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata?

o.en: The server author, since the MUST is written for the server
The end user, since consent metadata names what they saw
The platform or gateway operator, since it runs the process
The registry publisher, since metadata sits with a listing

x.en: The specification makes Protected Resource Metadata a server MUST, so without a gateway in front of it, the server author's own implementation is the one that has to carry it.

cite.text: MCP servers MUST implement OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata (RFC9728). MCP clients MUST use OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata for authorization server discovery.

q.en: A gateway now fronts that same server. Which role becomes responsible for validating the Origin header before a request reaches the server's own code?

o.en: The security and governance owner, who writes the policy
The gateway operator, who terminates the connection first
The server author, who still owns every transport check here
The host and client developer, who builds the OAuth client

x.en: Once a gateway terminates the connection, it is the first code to see the Origin header, so the platform or gateway operator inherits the MUST that the server author carried alone under plain HTTP.

q.en: A stdio deployment needs a credential for an internal API call. Per the specification's transport guidance, where should that credential come from?

o.en: An OAuth access token negotiated over the stdio channel itself
A bearer token embedded directly in the tool's input schema
The environment the operator configures before the process starts
A session id the server assigns on the connection's first call

x.en: STDIO implementations SHOULD NOT follow the OAuth authorization flow and instead retrieve credentials from the environment, which is the platform or gateway operator's responsibility to configure.

cite.text: MCP provides an Authorization framework for use with HTTP. Implementations using an HTTP-based transport SHOULD conform to this specification, whereas implementations using STDIO transport SHOULD NOT follow this specification, and instead retrieve credentials from the environment.

q.en: A curated requirement catalog includes a MUST whose default role is deliberately left unset because no single one of the six roles cleanly owns it. What should a responsibility matrix built from that catalog do with it?

o.en: Drop it from the matrix, since a MUST NOT is not a MUST
Assign it to the publisher by default, since it lists last
Assign it to the end user by default, since they consent
Report it as a gap so the team assigns an explicit owner

x.en: A responsibility matrix should surface an unowned MUST as a gap rather than guess an owner, because a silently misassigned requirement is as risky as an unassigned one.

q.en: A host and client developer needs an SDK that ships new protocol features before a spec release and resolves critical bugs within a week. Which SDK tier commits to that bar?

o.en: Tier 1, since it commits to full conformance and fast fixes
Any tier, since tiers only describe documentation quality, not speed
Tier 2, since six months is close enough for production use
Tier 3, since experimental SDKs move the fastest of the three

x.en: Tier 1 is the only tier that commits to shipping new features before or alongside a spec release and fixing critical bugs within seven days, the bar this scenario requires.

cite.text: Tier 1 SDKs are fully supported and implement every non-experimental feature, including optional capabilities such as sampling and elicitation. SDKs in Tier 2 are actively maintained and working toward full specification support, and those in Tier 3 are experimental, partially implemented, or specialized. Experimental features and protocol extensions (such as Tasks and MCP Apps) are not required for any tier.

q.en: Which factor most directly decides whether a capability should be exposed as a tool, a resource, or a prompt?

o.en: Whether the transport is stdio or Streamable HTTP, a detail the primitive never depends on
Who is meant to control it: the model, the application, or the user decide separately
How many bytes the response contains, a size limit no part of the protocol sets
Which language the server is written in, since MCP treats every runtime the same way

x.en: MCP assigns control of each primitive to a specific party: a tool is model controlled, a resource is application driven, and a prompt is user controlled, and that split is what a use case's initiator should decide.

questions.setTitle: Choosing MCP's Shape for the Job

cite.text: Prompts are designed to be user-controlled, meaning they are exposed from servers to clients with the intention of the user being able to explicitly select them for use. This refers to who decides when the prompt is used, not who authors its content. Prompt content is defined by the server.

q.en: A workflow automation use case kicks off a deploy pipeline that can run for twenty minutes before it finishes. Which result shape fits a request that long?

o.en: A normal complete result, because MCP places no ceiling on how long one response may take
A resource read that streams the growing output back as one ever-expanding text block
A CreateTaskResult from the tasks extension, returning a taskId the client polls to finish
An input_required result, because the client must supply an argument before anything can run

x.en: Work that risks a transport timeout is a good fit for the tasks extension, which returns a durable taskId and status instead of holding the connection open for the full duration.

questions.setTitle: Choosing MCP's Shape for the Job

cite.text: Tasks extend the standard request flow. When a server decides a request will be long-running, it returns a task handle instead of the final result. The client polls for completion.

q.en: A nightly CI job calls an MCP server with no human present to approve anything. Which authorization path fits that caller?

o.en: The interactive OAuth 2.1 code flow with PKCE, the same path a person would use
Dynamic Client Registration, completed once by a person before the nightly job ever runs
Credentials read from the environment, since every authorization path assumes a local stdio transport
The OAuth client credentials extension, which authenticates the machine caller with no user present

x.en: The OAuth client credentials authorization extension exists for exactly this case: an unattended, machine-to-machine caller that has no user available to complete an interactive redirect.

questions.setTitle: Choosing MCP's Shape for the Job

cite.text: The OAuth Client Credentials extension (`io.modelcontextprotocol/oauth-client-credentials`) adds support for the OAuth 2.0 client credentials flow to MCP. This enables automated systems to connect to MCP servers without interactive user authorization.

q.en: An internal ticket search tool's tools/list result is only meaningful within one authenticated organization. What must the result carry, and what does that setting not do?

o.en: cacheScope private, which limits sharing across contexts but is not an access control itself
cacheScope private, which the server also uses as its access control for this list
No cache fields, because the result stays scoped to the session opened earlier on
cacheScope public, because only server/discover results ever carry any caching hints at all

x.en: tools/list is one of the six cacheable operations and must carry cacheScope; private only limits sharing across authorization contexts, it does not itself enforce access control, and 2026-07-28 has no session to scope anything by.

questions.setTitle: Choosing MCP's Shape for the Job

cite.text: `"private"` | The response contains private data that is not meant to be shared between callers. Cached responses MAY be reused for the same authorization context. Caches MUST NOT be shared across authorization contexts (e.g. a different access token requires a different cache).

q.en: A function formats a currency string entirely inside one application process, with no external system, no separate host, and no second consumer. What does this scenario call for?

o.en: An MCP resource, so the application can read the formatted string as added context
A direct function call, since no external system or second consumer needs a protocol boundary
An MCP tool, so the model can invoke the formatter whenever a number appears
An MCP prompt, so the user can pick a formatting template from a menu

x.en: MCP's value comes from interoperability across hosts and servers; a capability with no second consumer and no separate system to standardize access to gains nothing from a protocol boundary.

questions.setTitle: Choosing MCP's Shape for the Job

q.en: A usage-dashboard tool ships an MCP Apps UI resource. A client that never declared the io.modelcontextprotocol/ui extension calls it. What should a well-behaved server do?

o.en: Reject the call outright, because a server treats every extension it offers as mandatory
Return the same interactive iframe, regardless of which capabilities the client happened to declare
Return a normal result with meaningful text, the fallback path for a client lacking it
Add the extension to the client's declared capabilities automatically so the call can proceed

x.en: Extensions are disabled by default and never assumed: a server offering a UI-enhanced tool should still return meaningful text content for a client that has not declared support for it.

questions.setTitle: Choosing MCP's Shape for the Job

cite.text: If one party supports an extension but the other does not, the supporting party MUST either revert to core protocol behavior or reject the request with an appropriate error if the extension is mandatory. Extensions SHOULD document their expected fallback behavior. For example, a server offering UI-enhanced tools should still return meaningful text content for clients that do not support the UI extension, while a server requiring a specific authentication extension MAY reject connections from clients that do not support it.

q.en: A team wants to add a capability beyond MCP's core primitives without colliding with anyone else who had the same idea. What must its extension identifier include?

o.en: A checksum computed over the settings object it carries
A numeric version suffix placed right after the name
A mandatory vendor prefix before the slash and name
A leading underscore marking the field as experimental

x.en: Extension identifiers follow vendor-prefix/extension-name, and unlike an ordinary _meta key the prefix is mandatory, so unrelated vendors and official extensions never collide on the same name.

cite.text: Extensions are identified using a unique _extension identifier_ with the format: `{vendor-prefix}/{extension-name}`, e.g. `io.modelcontextprotocol/oauth-client-credentials`. Identifiers follow the same rules as `_meta` keys, with a mandatory prefix. Official extensions use the `io.modelcontextprotocol` vendor prefix.

q.en: Under the 2026-07-28 revision, where does a client declare which extensions it wants active for one particular tools/call request?

o.en: In the initialize request's capabilities, sent once when the connection opens
In an Mcp-Extensions header attached to that same HTTP request
In a separate extensions negotiate call sent immediately before it
In that request's own _meta, under clientCapabilities extensions

x.en: There is no initialize handshake or session in 2026-07-28; a client declares its extensions fresh in _meta on every request, under io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities.extensions.

cite.text: This matrix shows which MCP clients support each official extension. Extensions are always opt-in: a client only uses an extension if both client and server declare support in the `extensions` field of their capabilities.

q.en: A client's request declares extensions A and B. The server's capabilities list extensions B and C. Which extension is active for this call?

o.en: Only B, because it is the one both sides named
None of them, because activation needs a separate confirmation step
A, B, and C, because declaring any of them activates all three
Only A, because the client is the one asking for behavior

x.en: An extension is active only when both the client's declared capabilities and the server's own capabilities name the same identifier, so the negotiated set here is just B.

cite.text: This matrix shows which MCP clients support each official extension. Extensions are always opt-in: a client only uses an extension if both client and server declare support in the `extensions` field of their capabilities.

q.en: A tool has no meaningful core-only behavior and only works with one specific mandatory extension active. A client calls it without that extension declared. What does a conformant server return?

o.en: A JSON-RPC error -32001, an old tool-failure code
A JSON-RPC error -32021, naming the extension it still needs
A JSON-RPC error -32601, because the method itself is unknown
A normal result with isError true and no other detail

x.en: A request that needs a capability, including an extension, that its own clientCapabilities did not declare is refused with MissingRequiredClientCapabilityError, -32021, naming what was missing in data.requiredCapabilities.

cite.text: A server MUST NOT rely on capabilities the client has not declared. If processing a request requires a capability the client did not include in `io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities`, the server MUST return a `MissingRequiredClientCapabilityError` (`-32021`) whose `data.requiredCapabilities` lists the missing capabilities. On HTTP, the response status MUST be `400 Bad Request`.

q.en: Before Core Maintainers will review a new official extension proposal at all, what must already exist?

o.en: A public vote among every registered MCP server operator
A full year of production traffic logged against the draft
A working reference implementation of it in an official SDK
A completed client support matrix showing every major client

x.en: An Extensions Track SEP must already have a reference implementation in an official SDK before the Core Maintainers will review it, unlike a Standards Track SEP.
