cite.text: *Entry. An Extension Maintainer, or the Working Group, submits an Extensions Track SEP under SEP-2133 and the SEP guidelines. It is reviewed like a Standards Track SEP, and SEP-2133 already requires it to identify the Working Group and Extension Maintainers and to have a reference implementation in an official SDK. When the SEP is accepted, the extension moves to `specification/beta/`, as Repositories and directories describes.

q.en: An official extension's maintainers need to remove a field, and the old and new behavior must keep working side by side under the same protocol revision. What should they do?

o.en: Ask every client vendor to update on the very same day
Wait for a twelve month deprecation window like a core feature
Publish the change quietly, since extensions evolve without core review
Ship it under a new identifier instead of the existing one

x.en: Per the extensions overview, a breaking change normally keeps the extension's identifier (Experimental and Beta extensions add or increment a revision string in their settings). A new identifier, for example with a -v2 suffix, is used only when old and new behavior must coexist under one protocol revision, as in this scenario.

review.note: Domanda riformulata: l'originale diceva che ogni modifica incompatibile richiede un nuovo identificatore, ma la pagina ufficiale sulle estensioni dice che l'identificatore resta lo stesso e ne serve uno nuovo solo se vecchio e nuovo comportamento devono coesistere. / Reworded: the original said every breaking change needs a new identifier; the official extensions page says the identifier is kept unless old and new behavior must coexist.

cite.text: Breaking changes keep the extension's identifier. A new identifier (e.g., `io.modelcontextprotocol/my-extension-v2`) is used only when old and new behavior must coexist under one protocol revision.

q.en: Why would a server reach for an interactive interface instead of returning ordinary tool content?

o.en: To let a user explore or configure something a paragraph of text cannot
To require a login step that completes before any tool call can run
To let the model silently rewrite the tool's own arguments before each call
To replace every text response in the conversation with one binary block

x.en: MCP Apps exists for results a user wants to explore or configure directly, such as drilling into a chart or filling out a form, not for content a plain text answer already serves well.

cite.text: MCP Apps let tools return rich, interactive interfaces instead of plain text. When a tool declares a UI resource, the host renders it in a sandboxed iframe, and users interact with it directly in the conversation.

q.en: Where does a client declare that it supports interactive interfaces before any resource is fetched?

o.en: In a dedicated `ui/register` call the client sends before any tool list
In `io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities.extensions` on the request
In the HTTP `Accept` header, listed alongside `text/event-stream` always
In a one-time `initialize` handshake both sides complete before any request

x.en: Extension support is declared per request in clientCapabilities.extensions, the same stateless pattern every capability in the 2026-07-28 protocol follows; there is no handshake or one-time registration call.

cite.text: This matrix shows which MCP clients support each official extension. Extensions are always opt-in: a client only uses an extension if both client and server declare support in the `extensions` field of their capabilities.

q.en: A tool definition carries `_meta.ui.resourceUri`. What does a host do with that field?

o.en: Treat it as a local template path bundled with the host application
Store it as the cache key for the tool's next `structuredContent` result
Fetch the `ui://` resource it names through an ordinary `resources/read`
Open the address in a new browser tab outside the conversation entirely

x.en: The field points at a ui:// resource, and a host resolves it the same way it resolves any other MCP resource, through resources/read, not through a special fetch method.

cite.text: `resourceUri`: The `ui://` scheme tells hosts this is an MCP App resource. The path structure is arbitrary. - `registerAppTool`: Registers a tool with the `_meta.ui.resourceUri` field. When the host calls this tool, the UI is fetched and rendered, and the tool result is passed to it upon arrival. - `registerAppResource`: Serves the bundled HTML when the host requests the UI resource. - Express server: Exposes the MCP server over HTTP on port 3001.

q.en: A host fetches a `ui://` resource and its `mimeType` comes back as plain `text/html`. What should the host conclude?

o.en: The resource is a valid app already, since its scheme is `ui://` at all
The resource is valid as long as its `_meta.ui.csp` domains are all trusted
The resource is valid because plain `text/html` is a safe default type
The resource is not a valid app; the required profile parameter is missing

x.en: Only text/html;profile=mcp-app marks a fetched resource as a renderable app; plain text/html is an ordinary HTML document the host should not treat as one, whatever the scheme says.

cite.text: This specification focuses on HTML content (`text/html;profile=mcp-app`) as the initial content type, with extensibility for future formats.

q.en: A host that never declared the interactive-interface extension calls a UI-capable tool anyway. What happens?

o.en: The tool still returns a normal result whose text content stays useful
The server silently upgrades the request as though the extension were declared
The call fails immediately with the unknown-method error `-32601`
The host receives an `input_required` result asking it to add the extension

x.en: A UI-capable tool keeps a meaningful text result for hosts that never declare the extension, and the side without support simply falls back to core behavior instead of the request failing.

cite.text: If one party supports an extension but the other does not, the supporting party MUST either revert to core protocol behavior or reject the request with an appropriate error if the extension is mandatory. Extensions SHOULD document their expected fallback behavior. For example, a server offering UI-enhanced tools should still return meaningful text content for clients that do not support the UI extension, while a server requiring a specific authentication extension MAY reject connections from clients that do not support it.

q.en: Why does an interactive interface render inside a sandboxed iframe instead of a directly embedded page?

o.en: So the app can freely reach the host page's cookies and local storage
So the app stays isolated from the host while privileged actions need consent
So the model can execute the app's own JavaScript in the host's context
So the server is allowed to skip returning any text content at all

x.en: The sandbox keeps the app from reaching the host page's cookies, storage, or DOM directly, so a host can render a server's app without auditing it line by line, while any privileged action still crosses a consent-gated bridge.

cite.text: MCP Apps run in a sandboxed iframe, which provides strong isolation from the host application. The sandbox prevents your app from accessing the parent window's DOM, reading the host's cookies or local storage, navigating the parent page, or executing scripts in the parent context.

q.en: When a team publishes a server to the MCP Registry, what does the registry actually store?

o.en: A cached copy of every tool description the server has ever returned
A cryptographic attestation that the server's code contains no security vulnerabilities
The server's own runtime logs, kept so a client can audit past tool calls
Metadata that names, versions, and locates the server, not the server's own code

x.en: The MCP Registry stores server.json metadata, name, version, and package or remote locations, and never hosts the server's own source code.

questions.setTitle: Finding, Routing To, and Trusting a Server

cite.text: The MCP Registry is the official centralized metadata repository for publicly accessible MCP servers, backed by major trusted contributors to the MCP ecosystem such as Anthropic, GitHub, PulseMCP, and Microsoft.

q.en: A publisher who has never proven ownership of the io.github.acme account tries to publish a server named io.github.acme/reporting-tool. What does the registry do?

o.en: Rejects the publish, since that namespace belongs to another verified owner
Accepts the publish, since anyone may choose any name they like
Publishes it but marks the version string as a prohibited range
Silently reassigns the name to a namespace the publisher does control

x.en: Namespace authentication ties a reverse DNS name to the specific GitHub account or domain that proved ownership of it, so a different publisher cannot claim it.

questions.setTitle: Finding, Routing To, and Trusting a Server

cite.text: This namespace system ensures that only the legitimate owner of a GitHub account or domain can publish servers under that namespace, providing trust and accountability in the ecosystem. For details on authentication methods, see the Authentication guide.

q.en: A server.json's $schema field points at the 2025-12-11 schema revision. What does that date tell you about the server itself?

o.en: The server refuses connections unless their date matches 2025-12-11 exactly
Nothing; the schema date and the protocol version are tracked separately
The server speaks MCP protocol version 2025-12-11 at the wire level
The server will stop working once the 2026-07-28 revision ships

x.en: A server.json's schema version describes the shape of the metadata document itself and is tracked completely separately from the MCP protocol version the server speaks at runtime.

questions.setTitle: Finding, Routing To, and Trusting a Server

cite.text: MCP Server Cards describe _remote_ MCP connectivity only. The MCP Registry's `server.json` separately describes registry entries, including locally installable packages and their runtime configuration. The Registry owns that schema; the Server Card extension does not define a `Server` superset or package-installation types.

q.en: A gateway receives a request whose Mcp-Method header says prompts/get, but the JSON-RPC body's method field says tools/call. What must the gateway do?

o.en: Trust the header for routing and let the body's method execute unchanged
Execute the body's method first, then correct the header in its response
Reject the request as a header mismatch before any backend is reached
Fall back to a legacy session so the two methods can be reconciled

x.en: Header and body must agree before a gateway routes or executes a request; a mismatch is rejected as HeaderMismatch with a 400 response before any backend is touched.

questions.setTitle: Finding, Routing To, and Trusting a Server

cite.text: Intermediaries that enforce policy based on mirrored headers (e.g., routing or rate-limiting by tenant) SHOULD verify that the `MCP-Protocol-Version` header indicates a version that requires header–body validation. If the version is older or the header is absent, the intermediary SHOULD reject the request rather than trusting unvalidated header values.

q.en: Two different authenticated callers both request the same private scope resource through a gateway. What is the correct caching behavior?

o.en: The gateway never caches a private scope result for any caller at all
The gateway serves the second caller's request from the first caller's cached entry
The gateway serves both callers from cache once the first request completes
The gateway fetches the resource again for each caller and never shares that entry

x.en: A private cacheScope result must never be shared across different callers, so the gateway fetches it again for each caller rather than reusing another caller's cached entry.

questions.setTitle: Finding, Routing To, and Trusting a Server

cite.text: `"private"` | The response contains private data that is not meant to be shared between callers. Cached responses MAY be reused for the same authorization context. Caches MUST NOT be shared across authorization contexts (e.g. a different access token requires a different cache).

q.en: An SDK rated Tier 1 then fails one conformance test on every run for five straight weeks. What happens to its tier?

o.en: It drops to Tier 2, since a sustained failure past four weeks relegates it
It stays at Tier 1, since one failing test is never enough to matter
It drops straight to Tier 3, since any conformance failure is treated as critical
It is removed from the tiering system until it is manually resubmitted

x.en: An SDK is relegated only after a conformance test fails continuously for four full weeks; five weeks of failure crosses that threshold and drops Tier 1 to Tier 2.

questions.setTitle: Finding, Routing To, and Trusting a Server

cite.text: An SDK may be moved to a lower tier if existing conformance tests on its latest stable release fail continuously for 4 weeks:

q.en: Before tracing an incident through an MCP transcript, which distinction should you check first to decide where the failure sits?

o.en: Whether the call happened over stdio only, since Streamable HTTP cannot produce this particular kind of failure
Whether the transcript runs longer than a handful of messages, since length alone predicts which particular domain a failure actually belongs to
Whether the connection kept a negotiated session open, since a lost session explains nearly every failure a server reports
Whether the message is a JSON-RPC error object with a code, or a normal result that instead carries isError true

x.en: A protocol error is a JSON-RPC error object with a numeric code, while a tool execution error is a normal result with isError true, and the two need different fixes from the model.

questions.setTitle: Reading One MCP Exchange End to End

cite.text: Tools use two error reporting mechanisms: Protocol Errors (unknown tool, malformed requests, server errors) are returned as standard JSON-RPC errors; Tool Execution Errors (API failures, input validation errors, business logic errors) are reported in tool results with isError: true.

q.en: A client configured for protocol version 2025-11-25 calls server/discover against this lesson's incident-console server. What happens next in a conformant 2026-07-28 exchange?

o.en: The server returns UnsupportedProtocolVersionError, and the client retries using a version the error itself names
The server downgrades every later request on the connection to match whatever version the client asked for first
The server opens a legacy initialize handshake so both sides can negotiate a shared version before anything else proceeds
The server silently applies its own default version and logs a warning that nobody is guaranteed to read later

x.en: A mismatched version returns error code -32022 with data.supported naming the versions the server accepts, and the client simply retries server/discover with a supported one, since there is no handshake or session to renegotiate instead.

questions.setTitle: Reading One MCP Exchange End to End

cite.text: Modern | Modern | Works. `server/discover` is optional; version mismatches surface as `UnsupportedProtocolVersionError` and the client retries with a mutually supported version.

q.en: bob-readonly sends restart_service with complete, valid arguments but declares no elicitation capability on that specific request. What does the server return?

o.en: A normal result with isError true, explaining that the environment argument bob supplied does not satisfy the schema
Error code -32021, MissingRequiredClientCapability, which explicitly names elicitation as the missing capability
resultType input_required anyway, trusting that bob will supply a client that can somehow still answer the elicitation
Error code -32602, since a caller missing a needed capability is treated the same as calling an unknown tool

x.en: A server must never assume a capability a request did not declare, so it answers with -32021, MissingRequiredClientCapability, and names exactly which capability was missing.

questions.setTitle: Reading One MCP Exchange End to End

cite.text: A server MUST NOT rely on capabilities the client has not declared. If processing a request requires a capability the client did not include in `io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities`, the server MUST return a `MissingRequiredClientCapabilityError` (`-32021`) whose `data.requiredCapabilities` lists the missing capabilities. On HTTP, the response status MUST be `400 Bad Request`.

q.en: alice's accepted restart_service retry carries the correct requestState but reuses the JSON-RPC id from the original ask. What is wrong with this retry?

o.en: The retry should have left requestState out entirely, since the server already has the original arguments recorded
The retry needed a shared session identifier instead of an id to prove it belongs to the same connection
The retry must use a brand new JSON-RPC id, since reusing the original id on a retry breaks the MRTR rule
Nothing; reusing the original id is exactly how a server is supposed to match a retry to its request

x.en: An MRTR retry always carries a new JSON-RPC id while echoing requestState exactly, so the id lesson 14 assigns to the original ask must never be reused on the retry that answers it.

questions.setTitle: Reading One MCP Exchange End to End

cite.text: The JSON-RPC `id` MUST be different between the initial request and the retry, as they are independent requests.

q.en: run_full_diagnostics is sent twice with identical arguments, once without declaring io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks and once declaring it. Why do the two calls return a different resultType?

o.en: The first call failed without telling the client, which then retried automatically with a different set of capabilities
The server alternates between a task and a synchronous result at random, purely to show the client both code paths
A task can only be created after the client has already polled tasks/get once to register interest in one
Capabilities are declared per request rather than for a whole connection, so only the request that opts in gets a task

x.en: MCP capabilities are declared per request, not once for a whole connection, so the server only returns resultType task when that specific request declares the tasks extension and it also advertised support for it.

questions.setTitle: Reading One MCP Exchange End to End

cite.text: A server MUST NOT rely on capabilities the client has not declared. If processing a request requires a capability the client did not include in `io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities`, the server MUST return a `MissingRequiredClientCapabilityError` (`-32021`) whose `data.requiredCapabilities` lists the missing capabilities. On HTTP, the response status MUST be `400 Bad Request`.

q.en: After a full run, one field on an early entry of the audit log is edited in place and audit.verify() is called again. What does it report?

o.en: False, naming the exact index of the edited entry, since its hash no longer matches what was recorded
True, because verify only ever recomputes the hash of the single most recent entry written to the log
False, naming the index of the entry recorded immediately before the one that was actually edited
True, because the edited field happens to fall outside what the hash function was actually designed to cover

x.en: Each entry's hash covers the entry before it, so editing one entry breaks the recomputed hash starting at that entry's own index, and verify reports precisely that index rather than the entry before it or a generic failure.

q.en: What is the primary purpose of Model Context Protocol (MCP)?

o.en: To limit the training data of AI models
To enable AI models to connect with external data sources, tools, and environments
To replace prompting when using Large Language Models
To create a new programming language for AI

x.en: Correct! MCP's main goal is to facilitate interoperability.

cite.text: Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open protocol that enables seamless integration between LLM applications and external data sources and tools. Whether you're building an AI-powered IDE, enhancing a chat interface, or creating custom AI workflows, MCP provides a standardized way to connect LLMs with the context they need.

q.en: What problem does MCP primarily aim to solve?

o.en: The lack of AI models
The high cost of training LLMs
The M×N Integration Problem
The difficulty in creating new AI algorithms

x.en: Correct! MCP standardizes connections to avoid M×N custom integrations.

cite.text: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open-source standard for connecting AI applications to external systems.

q.en: Which of the following is a key benefit of MCP?

o.en: Reduced AI model accuracy
Increased complexity in AI development
Standardization and interoperability in the AI ecosystem
Isolation of AI models from external systems

x.en: Correct! This is a primary goal and benefit of MCP.

cite.text: MCP takes some inspiration from the Language Server Protocol, which standardizes how to add support for programming languages across a whole ecosystem of development tools. In a similar way, MCP standardizes how to integrate additional context and tools into the ecosystem of AI applications.

q.en: In MCP terminology, what is a "Host"?

o.en: The external program exposing capabilities
The user-facing AI application
A read-only data source
A pre-defined template for interactions

x.en: Correct! The Host is the application users interact with.

cite.text: MCP Host: The AI application that coordinates and manages one or multiple MCP clients

q.en: What does "M×N Integration Problem" refer to in the context of AI applications?

o.en: The difficulty of training M models with N datasets
The challenge of connecting M AI applications to N external tools without a standard
The problem of managing M users across N applications
The complexity of developing M features for N different user segments

x.en: Correct! MCP provides the standard to solve this M*N complexity.

cite.text: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open-source standard for connecting AI applications to external systems.

q.en: What is the main purpose of the MCP SDKs?

o.en: To define the MCP protocol specification
To make it easier to implement MCP clients and servers
To provide a visual interface for MCP interactions
To replace the need for programming languages

x.en: Correct! SDKs abstract away low-level protocol details.

cite.text: Because MCP SDKs abstract away many concerns, most developers will likely find the data layer protocol section to be the most useful. It discusses how MCP servers can provide context to an AI application.

q.en: Which of the following functionalities do the MCP SDKs typically handle?

o.en: Optimizing MCP Servers
Defining new AI algorithms
Message serialization/deserialization
Hosting Large Language Models

x.en: Correct! This is a core function for handling JSON-RPC messages.

q.en: According to the provided text, which company maintains the official Python SDK for MCP?

o.en: Google
Anthropic
Microsoft
JetBrains

x.en: Correct! The course material indicates Anthropic maintains the Python SDK.

q.en: What command is used to start a development MCP server using a Python file named `server.py`?

o.en: python server.py run
mcp start server.py
mcp dev server.py
serve mcp server.py

x.en: Correct! This command initializes the development server.

q.en: What is the role of JSON-RPC 2.0 in MCP?

o.en: As a primary transport mechanism for remote communication
As the message format for all communication between Clients and Servers
As a tool for debugging AI models
As a method for defining AI capabilities like Tools and Resources

x.en: Correct! MCP uses JSON-RPC 2.0 for structuring messages.

cite.text: All messages between MCP clients and servers MUST follow the JSON-RPC 2.0 specification. The protocol defines these types of messages:

q.en: What is the primary role of an MCP Server in the Pull Request Agent architecture?

o.en: To host the user interface for the application
To expose tools and resources that the AI agent can use to interact with GitHub
To expose tools for reading and updating model repository tags on the Hugging Face Hub
To train the AI model on pull request data

x.en: Correct! The MCP Server provides get_current_tags and add_new_tag tools for Hub interactions.

cite.text: Hugging Face created an MCP server to make model management and dataset search a breeze.

q.en: In the FastMCP implementation, why must all MCP tool functions return strings instead of Python objects?

o.en: To improve performance by reducing memory usage
To ensure reliable data exchange between the MCP server and client
To make the code easier to debug
To comply with Hugging Face Hub API requirements

x.en: Correct! MCP protocol requires string responses, so we use json.dumps() to serialize data.

q.en: When implementing the `add_new_tag` tool, what is the purpose of checking if a tag already exists before creating a pull request?

o.en: To reduce API calls and improve performance
To prevent creating duplicate pull requests and provide better user feedback
To comply with Hugging Face Hub rate limits
To ensure the tag format is valid

x.en: Correct! This validation prevents unnecessary PRs and returns meaningful status messages.

q.en: In the MCP server implementation, what happens when a model repository doesn't have an existing README.md file?

o.en: The add_new_tag tool will fail with an error
The tool creates a new ModelCard with ModelCardData and proceeds with the tag addition
The tool skips adding the tag and returns a warning
The tool automatically creates a default README with placeholder content

x.en: Correct! The code handles HfHubHTTPError and creates a new model card when none exists.

q.en: What is the significance of using `create_pr=True` in the `hf_api.create_commit()` function call?

o.en: It makes the commit directly to the main branch
It automatically creates a pull request instead of committing directly to the main branch
It creates a private branch that only the repository owner can see
It validates the commit before creating it

x.en: Correct! This enables the review workflow and follows repository governance practices.

q.en: Why does the MCP server implementation use extensive logging with emojis throughout the code?

o.en: To make the code more fun and engaging for developers
To help with debugging and monitoring when the server runs autonomously in response to Hub events
To comply with FastMCP logging requirements
To reduce the amount of text in log files

x.en: Correct! Since the agent responds to webhooks automatically, detailed logs are crucial for troubleshooting.

q.en: What is the primary purpose of the webhook listener in the Pull Request Agent architecture?

o.en: To provide a user interface for managing pull requests
To receive and process Hugging Face Hub discussion comment events in real-time
To store pull request data permanently in a database
To authenticate users with the Hugging Face Hub

x.en: Correct! The webhook listener responds to Hub discussion events to trigger agent actions.

q.en: In the Agent-based MCP client implementation, how does the client connect to the MCP server?

o.en: Through direct function calls in the same process
Using stdio connection type to communicate with the MCP server as a subprocess
By writing files to a shared directory
Through HTTP REST API calls

x.en: Correct! The Agent starts the MCP server with 'python mcp_server.py' and communicates via stdin/stdout.

cite.text: In the stdio transport, the client launches the MCP server as a subprocess. The two ends communicate over the subprocess's standard streams:

q.en: Why does the webhook handler use FastAPI's `background_tasks.add_task()` instead of processing requests synchronously?

o.en: To reduce server memory usage
To comply with Hugging Face Hub requirements
To return responses quickly (within 10 seconds) while allowing complex tag processing in the background
To enable multiple webhook requests to be processed in parallel

x.en: Correct! Webhook endpoints must respond quickly or be considered failed by the sending platform.

q.en: What is the purpose of validating the `X-Webhook-Secret` header in the webhook handler?

o.en: To identify which repository sent the webhook
To prevent unauthorized requests and ensure the webhook is legitimate from Hugging Face
To decode the webhook payload data
To determine which MCP tools to use

x.en: Correct! The shared secret acts as authentication between Hugging Face and your application.

q.en: In the Agent implementation, what happens when `await agent_instance.load_tools()` is called?

o.en: It downloads tools from the Hugging Face Hub
It discovers and makes available the MCP tools from the connected server (get_current_tags and add_new_tag)
It starts the FastAPI webhook server
It authenticates with the Hugging Face API

x.en: Correct! This discovers what tools the MCP server provides and makes them available to the agent's reasoning engine.

q.en: How does the Agent intelligently use MCP tools when processing a natural language instruction?

o.en: It randomly calls available tools until one works
It always calls get_current_tags first, then add_new_tag second
It reasons about the instruction and determines which tools to call and in what sequence
It requires explicit function calls to be specified in the instruction

x.en: Correct! The Agent can understand complex instructions and create tool execution plans automatically.

q.en: What filtering logic determines whether a webhook event should trigger tag processing?

o.en: All webhook events are processed regardless of type
Only events where action='create' and scope='discussion.comment'
Only events from verified repository owners
Only events that contain the word 'tag' in the comment

x.en: Correct! This ensures we only process new discussion comments, ignoring other Hub events.
